INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Thirty Fifth Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
observations/recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Thirty First Report on Demands for 
Grants (2021-22) of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
2. The Two Hundred Thirty First Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok 
Sabha on 15 th March, 2021.  After presentation of the Report, the copies thereof were sent to the 
Ministry of Home Affairs on 15 th March, 2021 requesting them to furnish Action Taken Notes on 
the recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The Ministry of Home Affairs 
furnished the Action Taken Notes (in English) on 31 st August, 2021 and (in Hindi) on                            
1st December, 2021 on the above mentioned Two Hundred Thirty First Report to the Committee.   
3. The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuant to the direction of Chairman, Rajya Sabha dated                              
24th September 2004.     
 
4. The Committee considered the draft Two Hundred Thirty Fifth Report and adopted the 
same at its meeting held on 8th  December, 2021. 
 
5. The recommendations/observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.

CHAPTER-I 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
1.1 Overview 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee takes note of the ongoing vaccination process for COVID-19 and observes 
that, till now, less than 1% of the Indian population has been vaccinated and at this rate it will take 
many years to vaccinate whole population. The Committee also expresses its concern that a large 
number of people are missing the second dose of the vaccine. The Committee believes that it is 
very serious issue as the virus is mutating and new variants of COVID-19 are being reported in 
different parts of the world. The Committee therefore, recommends that all frontline health workers 
and the Corona Warriors including CAPFs and State/UT Police personnel receive the 
recommended doses of vaccine.  An attempt should be made to cover maximum people as early as 
possible.  
(Para 2.1.15 of 231st Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The COVID-19 vaccination drive was started on 16.01.2021 and around 38.76 crore 
beneficiaries across the country were successfully vaccinating within 180 days. All persons above 
the age of 18 years are eligible for COVID-19 vaccination since 1 st May 2021. The Revised 
guidelines for Implementation of National COVID vaccination Programme were announced on 7 th 
June, 2021 which has come in effect from 21 st June, 2021. Under the revised guidelines, 
Government of India is procuring 75% of the vaccines being produced by the manufacturers in the 
country which are being provided free of cost to States/UTs based on criteria such as population, 
disease burden and the progress of vaccination. These doses are to be administered by the 
States/UTs free of cost to all citizens aged 18 years and above as per priority through Government 
Vaccination Centres. Nearly 22% of the eligible population have received at least a single dose of 
COVID-19 vaccine, so far. 
1.1.3 The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has time and again issued advisories and 
emphasized at various platforms for States/UTs to ensure timely dose to the due beneficiaries as 
per the vaccination schedule for adequate protection. As per the coverage statistics on Co-WIN 
portal on 13 th July 2021, 90.9% of the Front-Line-Workers, which includes CAPFs, have been 
vaccinated with the 1st dose of COVID-19 vaccine and 51.4% have received the 2 nd dose. Similarly, 
among the Health Care Workers (HCWs), the 1st dose coverage is 87.5% and 2nd dose is 63.4%. 
1.1.4 The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare is holding regular meetings with States/UTs for 
increasing the pace of COVID-19 vaccination. As vaccine availability is likely to increase in the 
coming months, the coverage would increase significantly. 
1.1.5 The vaccination of all NDRF personnel including Medical & Para-Medical Staff has been 
done except some personnel who are suffering from various chronic diseases like TB, hypertension, 
asthma and allergy etc. A close monitoring is being taken to complete 100% vaccination in respect 
of all NDRF personnel as early as possible. 

4 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.6 The Committee note the significant progress made in the field of vaccination and 
appreciates the efforts of the Government.  The Committee hopes that the Govt. w ill achieve 
the desired result by the end of the year 2021. 
 
1.2 Allocations, Projections and Variations 
Recommendation 
 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that the total allocation for the Union Territories in BE 2021-22 is Rs. 
55,006.73 that is divided into two parts. i.e. Union Territories (without legislature) is Rs. 21,562.43 
crore and Union Territories (with legislature) are Rs. 33,444.30 crore. Further, for the Union 
Territories (without legislature), the allocation under the Revenue Head is Rs. 15,657.52 crore i.e. 
72.61% of the total allocation to the UTs and Capital Head is Rs. 5,904.91 crore i.e. 27.38% of the 
total allocation to the UTs. The Committee is of the considered view that the allocation under the 
Capital Head for the Union Territories (without legislature) should be increased for infrastructure in 
Health, Education, Agricultural, Energy and Allied sectors, Transport (connectivity), Development 
of Tourism, etc., in the UTs. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must review 
the capital requirements of these UTs and demand appropriate enhancement at RE stage to carry out 
developmental works in the UTs. 
(Para 2.2.5 ibid)

Recommendation 
 
1.2.11 The Committee notes that all UTs without leg islature have utilized around 62.25% of 
the total allocation made to them in RE 2020- 21. The Committee is aware that the UT of Ladakh 
was created last year and a separate budget allocation was made for its all-round development. B ut, 
the Committee is disappointed to note that in its first budgetary allocation, the UT of Ladakh has 
utilized just 27.42% of the allocation made in RE 2020-21. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the MHA should closely monitor the fund utilization by the UT of Ladakh in the ensuing year 
and take necessary corrective steps for enhanced utilization of funds in the UT. The Committee is 
of the strong view that the Union Territories of Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Chandigarh have 
optimally utilized the funds allocated to them and, therefore, should get their projected allocations 
from the Ministry of Finance. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Home 
Affairs may review the fund utilization status of every UT periodically and accordingly request 
additional funds from the Ministry of Finance at the RE stage. 
(Para 2.2.9 ibid) 

6 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.12 MHA has been continuously monitoring the expenditure by UT of Ladakh. However, the 
reason for less expenditure has been due to following reasons: 
i) Short working seasons in a year. 
ii) Stalling of activities due to Covid-19 Pandemic lockdown. 
iii) Working season lost in lockdown and unlock started in off season. 
iv) Ladakh depends on labour coming from outside. Due to lock down and pandemic 
related restrictions on movement of labour, the execution of works was affected. As a 
result of this, the responses to the tenders were also affected. 
v) Not having enough technical fields‘ staff such as draftsmen, JEs, AEs and AEEs with 
various State and Central executing agencies such as CPWD, NHIDCL and 
WAPCOS posted in Ladakh during this period. The said agencies also took some time 
to set up their offices in Ladakh during this period.  
vi) Inadequacy of local contractors in terms of men and machinery in UT of Ladakh. 
vii) A number of new big-ticket infrastructural projects are proposed to be taken up 
which requires comprehensive planning and specialist consultants for preparing 
DPRs. There is also a requirement of designing the projects keeping in view energy 
efficiency and various other aspects related to the region. The same required 
thorough consultation with stakeholders and expert agencies took due time during 
this period. 
1.2.13 In order to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness in execution of the projects and thereby 
maximise the utilisation of budgetary resources, several steps were taken: 
(i) Requisite Contract Committees and Local Purchase Committees have been 
constituted. 
(ii) Project Implementing Units (PIUs), Project Management Units (PMUs) and 
Consultants have been engaged for timely execution of various projects.  
(iii) Training of officers/staff conducted in GeM, PFMS, E-Office etc. 
(iv) Allotted 90 works to NHIDCL, 01 work to NBCC, 02 Works to WAPCOS and 14 
works to CPWD. 
(v) Ministry of Jal Shakti and CPWD have been approached for providing senior 
engineers on deputation. 
(vi) Government of J&K have been approached for deputation of officers viz. 
KAS/Planning/Finance and Engineers etc., for increasing the efficiency and 
effectiveness in execution of the projects.  
(vii)  Requisite staff/field functionaries at subordinate level have been engaged on 
outsourcing basis.

apply.

2.13 Landfill site at Ghazipur  
 
Recommendation 
 
2.13.1 The Committee expresses its concern about the landfill sites at Bhalsawa and Gazipur, 
which have been repeatedly expressed over the years.  The Committee observes that these sites 
continue to smoulder from time to time and releases toxic gases. Apart from stubble burning, 
landfill sites are also one of the factors for pollution of the air and the poor air quality in the 
National Capital.  The Committee recommends to increase the number of trommels to further 
reduce the height of dump at the landfill site of Bhalsawa and Ghazipur and allocate adequate funds 
for the same.  
(Para 5.7.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.13.2 Two Assistant Engineers (Civil) and four Junior Engineers (Civil) have been engaged on 
Sanitary Land Fill (SLF) site at Bhalsawa with other staff in shift-wise duty for 24 hours i.e. in 03 
shifts, who keep a check on any fire incident, and take suitable measures to douse the fire 
immediately.  Four (4) water tankers (2 water tankers of 9,000 litre capacity and 2 of 3,000 litre 
capacity) are available to deal with any situation of fire incident. Consequently, fire incidents have 
drastically reduced over the years. Year-wise fire incidents are as under: 
Year Number of fire incidents 
2016-17 98 
2017-18 131 
2018-19 99 
2019-20 32 
2020-21 02 
2021-22 03 
 
2.13.3 There is possibility of sudden eruption of fire due to landfill gases like methane etc. at 
Bhalsawa dumpsite. Hence eleven locations prone to such incidents have been identified. At each 
location 3.0-3.5 m chamber has been excavated. Steel grating has been placed at the bottom and 3 
‗250 mm DIA NP2‘ pipes vent have also been embedded. The pit/chamber has been filled with 
aggregate sand.  Thereafter, it has been sealed by cement concrete. The trapped gases are then 
flared in the air through these vent pipes to prevent fire incidents. 
2.13.4 At present, 24 trommels are functional at Bhalswa dumpsite and about 5,500 to 6,000 MT of 
legacy waste is being processed daily. Out of 80 lakh MT legacy waste, about 18.47 lakh MT has 
been cleared. First mound of 11 m height in an area of 14.90 acres from top has been completely 
cleared and clearing of second mound from top is in progress. About 23% of legacy waste has been 
cleared till 30.06.2021. To increase the processing capacity, number of trommels will be increased. 
As per the action plan, entire dump of legacy waste is likely to be cleared by June 2022.  
2.13.5 As per East Delhi Municipal Corporation (EDMC), in compliance of the order of Hon‘ble 
NGT (National Green Tribunal), the work of ―Hiring of segregation trommels for bio -mining and 
bio-remediation of old dump waste at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla dumpsites in Delhi‖ is in 
progress in East DMC.  At present, 20 trommels have been installed at SLF site Ghazipur. Legacy 

35 
 
waste to the tune of 7.10 lakh MT has already been processed. As and when space is created, more 
trommels will be installed. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
2.13.6 The Committee notes the reply.

Recommendation

3.6.33 Improvement in service condition/amenities and welfare of force personnel is a continuous 
endeavour. A study was got conducted in 2004 through Bureau of Police Research & Development 
(BPR&D) into the factors causing stress among force personnel and suggest the remedial 
measures. Another similar study was got conducted through Indian Institute of Management, 
Ahmedabad (IIMA) in 2012 for BSF and CRPF. 
3.6.34 On the basis of facts emerging from the studies, the measures taken to check incidents of 
suicides and to reduce the stress level of CAPFs and Assam Rifles (AR) personnel are as under:

and psychological concerns and organizing Meditation & Yoga routinely for better stress 
management. 
 Ensuring adequate rest and relief by regulating the duty hours. 
 Facility of retention of government accommodation at the place of last posting (for keeping the 
family) while posted in NE State, J&K and LWE affected areas (except State Capitals). 
 Transparent policies pertaining to transfer and leave of CAPFs and AR personnel. The 
hospitalization period due to injuries while on duty is treated as on duty. Choice posting is 
considered to the extent possible after the personnel served in hard area. 
 Regular interaction of officers with troops to find out and redress their grievances. 
 Improving living conditions for troops, providing adequate recreational/ entertainment, sports, 
communication facilities etc. Crèche facility is also provided at various establishments (where 
feasible) to facilitate the female employees. 
 Adequately compensating the troops deployed in difficult areas. 
 Other welfare measures like facility of Central Police Canteen renamed as Kendriya Police 
Kalyan Bhandar (KPKB), scholarship for wards etc. Also, air courier service has been 
provided to CAPF personnel deployed in NE States, J&K and LWE affected areas as welfare 
measure. 
 Designating retired CAPF personnel as ex-CAPF personnel for better identity and community 
recognition. 
 Promotions are released regularly to eligible personnel as & when the vacancies arise. 
Financial benefits under Modified Assured Career Progression (MACP) are given in case 
promotion does not take place for want of vacancies at 10, 20 & 30 years of service. 
 Organising Art of Living courses for CAPF personnel.

Recommendation 
 
3.12.1 The Committee is disappointed to note that only 27.42% of funds allocated to the UT of

53 
 
COVID-19 Pandemic restrictions, the progress in various developmental works have been affected.

Action Taken 
3.12.2 The UT of Ladakh has utilized 27.42% of the allocation made in RE 2020-21. The reasons 
for low spending of funds are as under: - 
a) Short working seasons in a year. 
b) Stalling of activities due to Covid-19 Pandemic lockdown. 
c) Working season lost in lockdown and unlock started in off season. 
d) Ladakh depends on labour coming from outside. Due to lockdown and pandemic 
related restrictions on movement of labour, the execution of works was affected. As a 
result of this, the responses to the tenders were also affected. 
e) Not having enough technical fields‘ staff such as draftsmen, JEs, AEs and AEEs with 
various State and Central executing agencies such as CPWD, NHIDCL and WAPCOS 
posted in Ladakh during this period. The said agencies also took time to set up their 
offices in Ladakh during this period. 
f) In-adequacy of local contractors in terms of men and machinery in UT of Ladakh. 
g) A number of new big-ticket infrastructural projects are proposed to be taken up which 
requires comprehensive planning and specialist consultants for preparing DPRs. There 
is also a requirement of designing the projects keeping in view energy efficiency and  
various other aspects related to the region. The same required thorough consultation 
with stakeholders and expert agencies took due time during this period. 
3.12.3 In order to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness in execution of the projects and thereby 
maximise the utilisation of budgetary resources, several steps were taken: 
i. Requisite Contract Committees and Local Purchase Committees have been constituted. 
ii. Project Implementing Units (PIUs), Project Management Units (PMUs) and 
Consultants have been engaged for timely execution of various projects. 
iii. Training of officers/staff conducted in GeM, PFMS, E-Office et c. 
iv. Allotted 90 works to NHIDCL, 01 work to NBCC, 02 Works to WAPCOS and 14 works 
to CPWD. 
v. Ministry of Jal Shakti and CPWD have been approached for providing senior 
engineers on deputation. 

54 
 
vi. Government of J&K have been approached for deputation of officers viz. 
KAS/Planning/Finance and Engineers etc. for increasing the efficiency and 
effectiveness in execution of the projects.

3.13 Power 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.13.1 The Committee observes that currently, the power generation in the UT is diesel based.  The 
spillage of diesel stored in power houses directly goes to the groundwater and affects the people 
living around. Therefore, it is important to shift from diesel base power generation to renewable 
power generation. Considering the small size of the UT, it can be fully powered through green 
energy.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Administration of UT of Lakshdweep may

Action Taken 
3.13.2 In Lakshadweep, electricity generation is mainly through diesel generators.  The diesel 
comes from the mainland, and the process of transportation is cumbersome thereby making it 
expensive.   The storage of diesel oil in barrels for long periods not only results in wastage of diesel 
but also affects the ecological condition of the coral islands. The cost of power per unit, thus 
become very high in Lakshadweep compared to other parts of the country. 
3.13.3 Keeping all these in mind, the Administration is in the process of building scientific storage 
system with the help of Indian Oil Corporation Limited. Initially, the two islands of Minicoy and 
Kavaratti, which are two of the Major islands for consumption of diesel for power generation, will

statutory procedures are completed. Similar projects for other islands (Andrott, Kalpeni, Agatti 
and Amini) are under progress. Accordingly, once the projects are completed, the difficulties arisen

55

3.13.5 However, UT of Lakshadweep Administration has now decided to go for privatization of

Demand No. 48 - Ministry of Home Affairs 
4.1 Glacial Outbursts 
 
Recommendation 
4.1.1 The Committee observes that excessive cutting of trees and use of dynamites on 
Hills/Mountains of the Himalayan region for roads, tunnels, dams and other 
developmental/infrastructural projects is significantly weakening the surrounding hills and may be 
causing an avalanche, landslides, flash floods and other catastrophes. The Committee understands 
that the Himalayas are fragile mountains and geologically and environmentally sensitive. 
Therefore, the developmental projects taking place in the region should be considered from the 
environmental and ecological point of view. The Committee recommends that the MHA may 
coordinate with the concerned agencies including NDMA, Ministry of Road, Transport & 
Highways, etc. to immediately ban the use of dynamites for developmental projects in the 
Himalayan region and make judicious use of technology particularly in high altitude Himalayan 
region to minimize the damage to ecology and environment. The Committee further recommends to 
explore technological solutions including use of cutting-edge technology and best practices 
followed by the other countries for cutting of hills/mountains for various developmental projects. 
(Para 3.8.11 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.1.2 Defence Research Geoinformatics Establishment (Ministry of Defence) has informed that 
the development of these areas will require roads, dams, tunnels etc. Hence use of explosives (used 
in mining) is very common for these developmental projects. To avoid any damage to mountains, 
controlled blasting, using specific quantity of explosive and delay detonators is a viable technology 
being used by advanced countries. The same is being used for mining, tunnelling etc. in our 
country. The commonly used material is gel explosive which is efficient and is being manufactured 
in our country. It is suggested that a careful use of explosives be done to achieve controlled 
blasting and avoid undue damage to hills. Also, techniques like hydro-seeding be used to achieve 
sustainable vegetation cover along with slope stabilization measures. M/o Road Transport & 
Highways (MoRTH) has also been asked to look into the matter and come up with a viable solution 
to the problem by using modern technology. MoRTH has sought views/ inputs from its executing 
agencies. 
4.1.3 As recommended by the Committee, the Government will make judicious use of modern 
technologies in this regard. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.1.4 The Committee notes the reply and would like to be informed about the progress made 
by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH) in finding a viable solution by 
using modern technology for developmental/infrastructural projects in Himalayan Region .

Demand No. 55 - Lakshadweep 
4.11 Fisheries  
 
Recommendation 
 
4.11.1 The Committee observes that the fishing potential of the UT of Lakshdweep is not being 
harnessed properly. The fishermen are not catching enough fish  due to lack of infrastructure like 
small crafts, ice plant, cold storage, processing units, etc. to catch, preserve and process fishes 
before they are sold in the market. The Committee is of the view that proper storage and processing 
unit will give fishermen the confidence that if the catch is not sold, at least it can be preserved, and 
can be sold in the market the next day. The Committee, therefore, recommends that investments 
should be made for creation of basic infrastructure to boost fishing industry in the UT to provide 
income security to the fishermen. The Committee is of the view that inland fisheries too have vast 
scope for the development of fisheries sector in the UT. The Committee, therefore,  recommends to 
utilize the available inland resources like ponds, swamps and low lying rain fed areas,  for fresh 
water fish farming through mariculture, cage culture and sea weed culture The Committee also 
recommends to increase budgetary allocation to develop fishery industry in the UT. 
(Para 5.6.28 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.11.2 The local fishermen of Lakshadweep islands use the most sustainable fishing method i.e. 
‗Pole & line‘. Now most of the fishing crafts have b een modernized in Maldivian style with craft 
size of 50 ft and above. Financial Assistance for construction / renovation of fishing small crafts 
and deep sea fishing vessels is also provided under UT Scheme.  In the FY 2021-22, UT of 
Lakshadweep Administration is taking action to develop post- harvest fish processing 
infrastructure facilities in various islands and  64% of the total Grant (GIA) of this current year 

71 
 
budget is earmarked for development of Fishery Infrastructure Development (FID). In addition to 
this, Rs.1.5 crore has been earmarked for cold chain development and establishment of fish 
handling centres in various islands. Similarly, five ammonia based ice plants have already been 
established at: Kavaratti, Kalpeni, Androth, Kadmath and Bitra. Besides, 3 numbers of 5 ton 
capacity Modern Containerized Ice Plants and 5 ton capacity cold storage have been installed at 
Agatti, Amini and Minicoy. Proposal for establishment of Cold storages, chilled rooms, ice plants 
and fish handling centres in various islands with the participation of private sector is also under 
consideration. As regards, quality insulated ice boxes, 65 boxes have been procured for free 
distribution to the fishermen and procurement of 235 boxes is also under process. Procurement and 
installation of Slurry Ice machines is also underway as a pilot project in Agatti.  
4.11.3 The Seaweed culture has been taken up as a pilot project with the technical support from 
Krishi Vigyan Kendra, Kavaratti. The Dept of Fisheries, UTL is implementing Marine Ornamental 
Fish culture project at Agatti with the support of National Cooperative Development Corporation  
(NCDC) and Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI), Kochi.   It has also been 
proposed to establish three Mini Fish Processing Centres in Minicoy, Agatti & Kitlan. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.11.4 The Committee notes that various measures that are being taken for developme nt of 
the fisheries infrastructure in the UT of Lakshadweep. The Committee, however, desires to be 
apprised about the measure taken to utilize  the  available inland  resources  like  ponds,  
swamps  and  low-lying  rain  fed  areas, for  fresh  water  fish farmin g  through  mariculture,  
cage  culture  and  sea  weed  culture.

police force will be adversely affected due to such vacancies.  The Comm ittee, therefore, 
recommends that the matter may be pursued with SSC to speed up the process of recruitment 
to fill the identified vacancies. 
(Para  3.6.10) 
 The Committee further notes that the process for filling up of  around 700 posts of 
Gazetted Officers (Assistant Commandants and above)against the vacancies of 2,096 posts 
has been initiated.  The Committee observes that there is a gap of more than 1300 posts of 
GOs in CAPFs.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation at para 4.3.25 of 
the 231st Report and recommends that all the vacancies at senior grades should be filled up on 
urgent basis as this has a direct bearing on the decision making capabilities of the forces.  
(Para  3.6.11) 
 The Committee appreciates that BSF has started accepting Residence Certificate of 
UT of Ladakh issued by the concerned authority till the rules related to domicile certificate 
are notified.  However, no response on the decision taken on problem related to medical 
testing of the candidates has been furnished. The Committee, therefore, reit erates its 
recommendation at para 4.3.27 of 231st Report. 
(Para 3.6.15) 
 
 The Committee notes that sensitization-cum-awareness workshop for CISF per sonnel 
have been conducted only at four airports i.e. New Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai. 
Committee also notes that a system of regular briefing to security officials has been initiate d 
and on-job trainings are imparted to CISF personnel at the airports.  However, such 
sensitization-cum-awareness workshops for CISF personnel should cover all the airports and 
not just confined to New Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai.  The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation at para 4.3.28 of 231st Report.   
(Para  3.6.20) 
 
 The Committee notices that steps taken to encourage representation of women in  
CAPFs have resulted in the increase in number of women personnel from 20,568 on                        
1st February, 2016 to 34,778 on 25 th August, 2021 and thus 14,210 additional women 
personnel have been recruited in CAPFs in five years. The Committee fur ther recommends 
that awareness-cum-interactive sessions in schools, colleges and other educational 
institutions, could be organized to further encourage the young women to consider joinin g 
CAPFs. 
(Para  3.6.25) 
 
 
 The Committee notes the various measures being taken to improve the housing 
satisfaction level in CAPFs.  The Committee takes notes about the construction of 23,456 
houses by the Government of  India.   The Committee also observes that there is still a huge 
gap between the need and availability of houses for the personnel and therefore, f eels that the 
MHA may ensure that the measures taken by them translates into the improved housing 
satisfaction level of CAPFs personnel.  For this purpose, a roadmap may be put in place 

82 
 
coupled with regular monitoring, so that the same may be completed within the stipulated 
time frame to avoid cost overruns. 
(Para  3.6.28) 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the routine reply that the policy will be reviewed 
at per requirement in future.  The Committee has already delineated the need to review the 
number of leaves given to the CAPFs personnel.  The Committee strongly believes that CAPF 
personnel below the Officers Rank should be given leaves at par with the Army Personnel.  
The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation at para 4.3.34 of the 231st Report. 
(Para  3.6.31) 
 The Committee notes that two studies were conducted in the year 2004 and 2012, 
respectively, through BPR&D and Indian Institute of Management, Ahmadabad. The 
Committee also notes that based on these studies, remedial measures have been taken to 
reduce the stress level in CAPFs and Assam Rifles personnel in order to check  the incidence 
of suicides. The Committee however is of the view that as  approximately 12 years and 9 
years, respectively have elapsed since these studies were undertaken and also the fact that a 
lot of new challenges has emerged in their field of duty, there is an urgent ne ed to review and 
reassess the situation in view of the increasing number of suicide cases among the CAPF 
personnel. 
(Para  3.6.35) 
 
Railway line between Bilaspur (H.P) & Leh 
 
 The Committee notes the reply.  However, the Committee observes that the prop osed 
project of railway line between Bilaspur (H.P.) and Leh is at a nascent stage and the process 
needs to be speeded up to bring the project into reality.  MHA may, therefore, take up the 
matter with the concerned Ministries/Departments/Organisations so as to work out a 
roadmap for execution of the project. 
(Para  3.7.3) 
 
Delhi Police 
 
 The Committee observes that only 87 staff quarters could be completed in the 
financial year 2020-21 as against the planned  345  staff quarters due to COVID-19 Pandemic 
and lockdown.  The Committee also notes that the Ministry is contemplating to complete the 
construction of 258 staff quarters in the financial year 2021-22.  However, the Committee is 
deeply disappointed to note that after completion of these projects, the housing satisfaction  
level in Delhi Police will increase to 22% in the Financial Year 2022-23 and approximately 
30% only in the Financial Year 2025-26, subject to the condition that no new posts are 
created during this period in Delhi Police.  The Committee observes that there would still be a 
huge gap between the need and availability of accommodation for Delhi Police personnel. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends to expedite the whole process to attain at least 50% 
housing satisfaction level in Delhi Police by the FY 2025-26.   
(Para  3.8.10) 
 
 The Committee also observes that 254 completed flats could not be handed ove r to 
Delhi Police as the payment is to be made to DDA.  The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of Finance may be requested to enhance the allocation at an appropriate stage  so 
that the process of acquiring these flats could be expedited.   

83 
 
(Para 3.8.11) 
 
 
National Investigation Agency (NIA)

of working in ATS/STF. The Committee, however, is deeply concerned to n ote that one of the 
reasons for existing vacancies in NIA is on account of CAPF personnel not being eligi ble to 
apply for posts in NIA due to internal regulation of quota. The Committee recom mends that 
bottlenecks may be sorted out and a decision on fixing quota from CAPFs in NIA  be taken up

regard.    
(Para  3.9.5)

(WARB) under MHA and Department of Pension & Pensioner‘s Welfare (DoP&PW) to

However, it is also noted that the Ministry has not given any clear reply to the Committee‘s 
recommendation regarding the steps taken for mitigating the socio-economic harships faced 
by the parents of the martyred personnel.  It has also not given a clear cut reply to whether 
any decision has been taken for making necessary provisions for such parents so that they 
may be entitled a share in the pensionary benefits. The Committee, therefore, reite rates its 
recommendation at para 4.12.7 and urges the Ministry to look into the matter expeditiously 
and apprising the Committee about its progresses.   
(Para  3.10.3) 
 
Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems(CCTNS) 
e-FIR 
 
 The Committee notes that on 14 th September, 2018, NCRB sent an advisory to 
States/UTs for customizing and use the e-FIR module as per their requirement. But, e- FIR 
facility is currently available only in Delhi, Odisha, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. The

including Zero-FIRs are being registered electronically using CCTNS in 15,890 Police 
Stations.  The Committee, observes that there is a need to synchronize the portals being use d 
by the States for registration of FIR on their website with the CCTNS so as to create a 
comprehensive data bank on crime and criminals.  The Committee  urges u pon the Ministry 
to take up the matter with the Home Secretaries of all the States and UTs on quarterly basis 
and impress upon them the need for expeditious implementation of CCTN in the resp ective 
State/UT.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Thirty S ixth Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations Contained in the Two Hundred Twenty Ninth Report on the 
'Management of COVID-19 Pandemic and Related Issues'. 
 
2. The Two Hundred Twenty Ninth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was virtually presented through video conferencing to the Hon'ble 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 21 st December, 2020 and was forwarded to the Hon’ble Speaker, Lok 
Sabha on the same day. Thereafter, the said Report was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the 
Table of the Lok Sabha on the 2 nd February, 2021.  After virtual presentation of the Report to the 
Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha and forwarding the same to the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha on 21 st 
December, 2020, the copies thereof were sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs requesting them to 
furnish Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The 
Ministry furnished the Action Taken Notes on the said Report to the Committee on 30th July, 2021.  
 
3. The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuant to the direction of Chairman, Rajya Sabha dated                               
24th September 2004.     
 
4. The Committee considered the draft Two Hundred Thirty S ixth Report and adopted the same 
at its meeting held on 8th December, 2021. 
 
5. The recommendations/observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.

 The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of 
Home Affairs on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred and Twenty Ninth Report of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs on the 'Management of 
COVID-19 Pandemic and Related Issues'. The 229 th Report of the Committee was virtually presented 
through video conferencing to the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 21 st December, 2020 and was 
forwarded to the Hon‟ble Speaker, Lok Sabha on the same day. Thereafter, the said Report was 
presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha on the 2nd February, 2021. 
 
2. In view of the importance and sensitivity of the subject, the Committee held a meeting on 28 th 
June, 2021, to keep itself abreast of the latest situation in the country and steps taken by the 
Government of India on the recommendations made by the Committee in its 229 th Report. In the 
meeting, the representatives of the MHA, Ministries of Finance, Commerce & Industry, Health & 
Family Welfare and Labour & Employment briefed the Committee on the „Socio -Economic Fallout of 
the COVID-19 Pandemic‟s Second Wave‟. The Committee was informed about the rise in COVID -19 
case in different places in different time; implementation of micro containment strategy at the district, 
city level;  localised lockdowns; coordination with States/UTs by providing overall guidance; number 
of cases, deaths, recovery rate and case fatality rate; institutional arrangeme nts and advisories issued to 
manage the second wave; challenges faced during second wave; five-fold strategy of test- track-treat-
vaccination and adherence to COVID-19 appropriate behaviour; status on production of vaccines; 
infrastructure, testing, local containment and clinical management; efforts to fulfil augmented oxygen 
demand; guidelines for preparedness on paediatric care; release of funds to States under State Disaster 
Relief Fund (SDRF); augmentation of health infrastructure; extension of Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan 
Package by 180 days for the intended beneficiaries; vaccination drive; economic recovery post-second 
wave; food procurement/distribution and employment generation under MNREGA, etc.

1.1 India's Preparedness to Tackle the Pandemic 
 
Outcomes/Gains/Effectiveness of strategies adopted to manage the Pandemic 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee, however, observes that the sudden imposition of lockdown necessitated by the 
challenging situation and the fear of the rapid spread of the virus did result in unprecedented disruption. 
The lockdown led to the stoppage of Intra-State and Inter-State movement of people, goods, shutdown 
of factories, hotels, eateries, tourism, etc., and other economic activities that led to unprecedented 
disruption and severe social and economic fallouts. The migrant labourers, factory workers, daily wage 
earners were the worst affected. The civil administration in the States and the districts prepared to 
respond to the challenge and establish shelters and quarantine facilities. As there was no timely 
dissemination of the information in the district areas about the arrangements being made for food, 
shelter and other facilities, anxiety and uncertainty gripped the migrant labourers and workers and led 
to their movement in large number to their home States. This stopped only when effective mitigating 
measures were taken by Central and the State Governments. 
(Para 2.6.12 of the 229th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The observations of the Hon‟ble Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) have been noted. 
 
1.1.3 MHA issued regular advisories to States/UTs to take all necessary measures to provide shelters, 
food, water, health facilities and also proper counselling to migrant workers. 
 
1.1.4 On 28 th March, 2020, Central Government allowed State Governments to use SDRF for making 
provisions of temporary accommodation, food, clothing, medical care, etc., to homeless people 
including migrant labourers. To augment the funds with the States, Central Government released in 
advance Rs.11,092 crores from the SDRF to the States on 3rd April, 2020 itself. 
 
1.1.5 On 19 th April, 2020 movement of migrant workers was allowed within the States/ UTs so that 
they could be engaged in industrial, farming, construction, manufacturing and MNREGA works as 
additional new activities were permitted outside containment zones with effect from 20th April, 2020. 
  
1.1.6 On 29 th April and 1 st May 2020, MHA further allowed the movement of migrant workers to 
their native places by buses and Shramik special trains respectively. MHA facilitated the movement of 
migrant workers to their native places through Shramik special trains in coordination with the Indian 
railways and State/ UT Governments. More than 64 lakh migrant workers were transported by Indian 
Railways in a smooth manner. 
 
 
 

4 
 
Further Deliberations of the Committee 
 
1.1.7 In the meeting of the Committee held on 28 th June, 2021, to examine the  Socio-Economic 
Fallout of the COVID-19 Pandemic’s Second Wave’,  the Home Secretary informed the Committee that 
the second wave of Pandemic came with cases rising at different times in different places of the 
country.  Therefore, micro containment strategy in consultation with the Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare was devised and implemented at the district level. Instead of going for  national level changes, 
States were asked to do it at the local level.  The Centre played a key role in providing the overall 
guidance to the States and UTs.  Based on this, States implemented their own measures based on the 
assessment of the local situation, evidence based real time dynamics approach of imposing restrictions, 
etc.  The situation was reviewed in the country at the highest level on regular basis.  The Ministry of 
Home Affairs issued orders, guidelines and advisories from time to time to ensure this containment of 
COVID-19 in the country.  Before the second wave started, on 23 rd March, 2021 MHA had issued the 
guidelines to States to keep a watch, impose restrictions at district, sub-district level and strict 
enforcement of COVID appropriate behavior with a view to contain spread of COVID-19.    Before the 
second wave started, the MHA emphasized on the strategy of test, track, and treat protocol with micro-
containment zones across the States during Virtual Conferences with the Chief Secretaries as well as in 
meetings of Hon’ble Prime Minister with the Chief Ministers.  The MHA subseque ntly issued various 
advisories in the month of March itself, generating awareness on COVID appropriate behavior.  
Thereafter, guidelines were issued on 29 th April, 2021 where States and UTs were asked to consider 
containment measures as per the advisory of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare which was issued 
on 25th of April, 2021.  On 19 th June, the States were advised for a five-fold strategy when the numbers 
came down and activities were opened in a calibrated manner.  It was also advised to increase the 
pace of testing and keep a close watch on any signs of surge at the local, district, city and micro-
subdivision level and take measures to check it right. 
 
1.1.8 For disbursement of funds to States, the MHA has allowed State Governments to use 10 percen t 
of their opening balance of State Disaster Relief Fund (SDRF) for COVID containment measures.  
However, when the surge increased in April, 2021, the percentage was increased to 50 percent of the 
SDRF. More than Rs. 8,800 crores were released to the States as first installment as a Central share. 
The States add their own share and then they could use 50 percent of it for COVID containment 
measures.

2.1 India's Preparedness to Tackle the Pandemic  
 
Outcomes/Gains/Effectiveness of strategies adopted to manage the Pandemic 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.1.1 The Committee observes that several steps were taken much ahead of what many other 
countries took subsequently for the screening of travellers and passengers coming from abroad into 
India. All international flights were also prohibited in a graded manner. While doing so, the Central 
Government was conscious of the need to bring back stranded Indian citizens abroad to the safety of 
their homes. The Committee, however, observes that incoming international passengers including those 
who entered throughout March, 2020 were screened only for high temperature and there was no testing 
facility established at the airports. Thus, asymptomatic patients as also those who travelled after taking 
medicines for controlling temperature could not be diagnosed at a time when they could practically be 
the only source of infections of COVID-19 in the country. 
 
(Para 2.6.9 of the 229th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.1.2 After Government of India decided on universal screening of all international travelers on 6 th 
March 2020, around 50 to 60 thousand passengers were being screened daily until cessation of all 
flights on 22 nd March 2020. At that time, there were just over 100 laboratories all across the country, 
with a daily capacity to test 15000 samples a day was available with the country. Given the limited 
resources available at that point of time, testing of every international traveler was not a fea sible 
strategy. However, Government of India ensured that travelers, after reaching their destination are kept 
under surveillance and followed up for 28 days. 
 
2.1.3 Also, the persons brought under Government of India‟s initiative for medical evacuation of 
Indians from COVID affected countries (such as China, Iran, Italy, Japan etc.) were ke pt under 
institutional quarantine for 14 days and were all tested negative for COVID-19 before relea se from 
quarantine. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.1.4 The Committee notes the reply.

COVID-19 Pandemic and understands that the primary effect of nationwide lockdown was to have a 
uniform set of regulations, to delay peak infections and provide time to the health system to mop up

ramp up its public health infrastructure, build the capacity of hospitals and health care workers. The 
Committee also understands that one of the key elements of the Pandemic control strategies across the

varying degrees of stringency.

3.1 India's Preparedness to Tackle the Pandemic 
 
Outcomes/Gains/Effectiveness of strategies adopted to manage the Pandemic 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.1.1 From the benefit of the experience gained while addressing these challenges, the Committee 
recommends that the Government should draw up a national plan and guidelines under NDMA, 2005 
and Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897. An effective functional institutional mechanism is needed for co-
ordination between the Centre, States and Union Territories for quick response to such a crisis in 
future. This would ensure efficacious implementation of all decisions to contain Pandemics and 
equitable/timely distribution of relief at district and sub divisional levels to the intended beneficiaries in 
urban and rural areas. 
(Para 2.6.13 of the 229th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 NDMA had prepared National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP) in May, 2016 as per the 
provisions of the Disaster Management Act (DM Act), 2005. NDMP was revised in November, 2019. 
The Plan inter – alia, mentions, specific measures at the Centre and State level required for mitigation 
and preparedness for Biological Disasters and Public Health Emergencies. The Plan contains a chapter 
on Biological Disasters and Pubic Health Emergencies, from which specific plan for any specific 
Biological Disaster has to be formulated by the concerned Ministry. It contains responsibility 
framework on Biological and Public Health Emergencies at Section 7.15 with six different components 
for disaster risk reduction. The Plan, inter – alia, mentions that Ministry of Health & Family Welfare is 
the nodal Ministry for dealing with biological emergencies. Work done by NDMA with regard to 
guidelines is given below: 
 
(i) In October, 2007, National Disaster Management Authority released National 
Guidelines on Medical Preparedness and Mass Casualty Management. 
(ii) In July, 2008, NDMA issued guidelines on Biological Disasters. 
(iii) In December, 2009, NDMA issued guidelines on Psycho-social support and mental 
health services in disasters. 
(iv) In August, 2010, NDMA issued guidelines on Management of the Dead in the aftermath 
of Disasters. 
(v) In February, 2016 NDMA issued guidelines on Hospital Safety. 
(vi) NDMA released „Guidelines on Influenza A (H1N1) Pandemic Preparedness for 
Business Continuity in Non- Health Sectors‟. Further, an „Action Plan on Pandemic 
Preparedness and Response‟ was also released by Ministry of Health an d Family 
Welfare in consultation with NDMA in May 2009. 
 

37 
 
3.1.3 The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 was enacted to provide for better prevention of the spread of 
dangerous epidemic diseases. In the present Epidemic Diseases Act the Central Government has been 
given a concurrent role with the State Governments to take any measures that may be needed to prevent 
the outbreak of an epidemic like current COVID-19 or the spread thereof. Further, Public Health be ing 
state subject, the Section 2 of Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 empowers the State Government to 
prescribe regulations to be observed by the public to prevent the outbreak of any dangerous epide mic 
disease or the spread thereof if, it thinks that ordinary provisions of the law in force are insufficient for 
the purpose. 
 
Further Deliberations of the Committee 
 
3.1.4 In the meeting of the Committee held on 28 th June, 2021, to examine the  Socio-Economic 
Fallout of the COVID- 19 Pandemic’s Second Wave’ t he representative of National Disaster 
Management Authority (NDMA) highlighted its efforts in management of second wave which included 
several meetings with States and Ministries of Labour & Employment, Panchayati Raj, Housing & 
Urban Affairs, Departments of Skill Development, Pharmaceuticals, Economic Affairs, Land Resources 
and Non-Government Organizations (NGOs), etc., for the management of Pandemic; tracing and 
tracking of COVID-19 positive persons through IT Enabled Integrated Hotspot Analysis System 
(Itihas) portal; counseling of people through psycho-social care portal; addition of equipments in India 
Disaster Resource Network (IDRN), etc. The NDMA has also interacted with more than 1000 NGOs to 
discuss various issues regarding management of the Pandemic.   
 
3.1.5 The attention of the Committee was drawn to the practical difficulties faced by the health 
workers of the PHCs, hospitals, etc. It was pointed out that at the time of such emergencies, extensive 
paperwork have acted as an hindrance for providing emergency healthcare to the affected patients to 
the extent that at some places, it led to piling up of dead bodies awaiting clearance of the doctors. 
Hence, the Committee has opined that the need for paperwork for providing healthcare facilities to the 
patients should be looked in to and addressed properly so that the patients are extended healthcare 
facilities quickly during the Pandemics like COVID-19. The Ministry of Home Affairs, in its reply, 
acknowledged and clarified the matter and assured to take appropriate steps in this regard. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.1.6 The Committee notes that NDMA had prepared the National Disaster Management Plan 
(NDMP) in May, 2016 which was revised in November, 2019, i.e. before the onset of COVID-19 
Pandemic in India. Therefore, the Committee further recommends that the NDM A may revise 
NDMP to include the lessons learned and experience gained in the management of COVID-19 
including SOPs, lockdowns, public health management, etc. Accordingly, NDMA along with the 
Ministry of Health & family Welfare may issue fresh/additional guidelines/Standard Oper ating 
Procedures (SOPs) for curbing and managing Pandemics in future.  
  
3.1.7 The Committee also recommends that the National Disaster Management Act (NDMA), 
2005 may be suitably amended to include a clause ‘subject to correction’ during digital data 
collection and reduction in paperwork for extending benefits, etc., to the intended beneficiaries.

3.2 Augmentation of Health Infrastructure 
 
Adequacy of such assistance to States/UTs 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.1 The Committee observes that the Pandemic has pushed both Central and State Governments to 
incur heavy expenditure on COVID-19 treatment and related services. The Committee is of the  view 
that the public sector healthcare delivery system needs to be further strengthened in all the States/ UTs 
and a uniform healthcare system should be established across the country to deal with the Pandemic on 
a sustained basis in future. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in the long term, there should 
be more investments in health infrastructure for the rapid scaling up of public health services. A strong 
and effective public health infrastructure is necessary to respond to such a Pandemic due to which 
thousands of COVID-19 patients are getting admitted to hospitals in addition to the non-COVID-19  
patients. 
(Para 3.10.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.2.2 In a bid to further improve public health funding, a new centrally sponsored scheme, PM Atma 
Nirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojana, has been announced with an outlay of about Rs. 64,180 crores over 6

existing national institutions, and create new institutions, to cater to detection and cure of new and 
emerging diseases. The main interventions under the scheme are: 
 
(i)   Support for 17,788 rural and 11,024 urban Health and Wellness Centers 
(ii) Setting up integrated public health labs in all districts and 3382 block public health units 
in 11 states; 
(iii) Establishing critical care hospital blocks in 602 districts and 12 central institutions; 
(iv) Strengthening of the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), its 5 regional branches 
and 20 metropolitan health surveillance units; 
(v) Expansion of the Integrated Health Information Portal to all States/UTs to connect all 
public health labs; 
(vi) Operationalisation of 17 new Public Health Units and strengthening of 33 existing Public 
Health Units at Points of Entry, at 32 Airports, 11 Seaports and 7 land crossings; 
(vii) Setting up of 15 Health Emergency Operation Centers and 2 mobile hospitals; and 
(viii) Setting up of a national institution for Health, a Regional Research Platform for WHO 
South East Asia Region, 9 Bio-Safety Level III laboratories and 4 regional National 
Institutes for Virology.

Further Deliberations of the Committee 
 
3.2.14  When asked about the shortage of liquid medical oxygen during second wave in the 
meeting of the Committee held on 28 th June, 2021, to examine the  Socio-Economic Fallout of the 
COVID-19 Pandemic’s Second Wave’, the representative of Department for Promotion of Industry and 
Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce & Industry apprised the Committee that during second 
wave, there was rapid surge in the active cases which resulted in sudden and enormous spike in the 
requirement of medical oxygen. The daily average on a monthly basis, liquid medical oxygen supply 
was 1,292 metric tons in February 2021, 1,459 metric tons in March, 2021. It rose to almost 5000 
metric tons in April, 2021 which further increased to 8,520 metric tons on daily basis in the month of 
May, 2021. Therefore, the production of liquid medical oxygen was increased to match the sudden 
increase of demand. The measures taken to increase oxygen supply inter-alia included enhancing their 
production and supply including capacity in the public sector units, import of oxygen, reduction in 
safety stocks requirement of the steel plants from three-and-a-half days to half a day, thereby making 

41 
 
available thousands of tons of liquid oxygen for medical purposes.   The use of liquid oxygen for 
industry was also restricted.  The liquid medical oxygen was transported to various parts of the country 
through railways, air force, navy, etc. 
   
3.2.15  The Home Secretary, further informed the Committee that during second wave of 
COVID-19, huge quantum of oxygen was mobilised from Eastern part of the country to the Northern 
and Western parts of the country where it was in short supply as the production is mostly in steel plants 
located on the Eastern side.  The MHA banned use of liquid medical oxygen by any other industry 
temporarily and diverted all oxygen that was produced in the country for use of medical purposes.    
 
3.2.16  The Home Secretary further informed the Committee that to augment the funds to the 
States, MHA had allowed State Governments to use 10 percent of their opening balance of State 
Disaster Relief Fund (SDRF) for COVID containment measures.   However, when the surge increased 
in April, 2021, the percentage was increased to 50 percent of the SDRF. More than Rs. 8,800 crores 
were released to the States as first installment as a Central share. The States may add their own share 
and then they could use 50 percent of it for COVID containment measures.  
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.17  The Committee observes that the nature and virulence of the COVID-19 Pandemic 
is unpredictable. Hence, alertness and preparedness cannot be compromised at any stage. The  
Committee, therefore, recommends that the MHA may advise the States that the COVID-19 
infrastructure facilities including testing facility, ICU beds and medical oxygen created for  
patients may not be scaled down completely as given the deceptive nature and emergence  of 
multiple variants, the virus may give rise to a third wave without giving sufficient time to react. 
They should be kept in a dormant state so that they can be reactivated to deal with the 
subsequent wave of the Pandemic that might come up. 
  
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.18  The Committee strongly recommends that there is a need for a comprehensive Public 
Health Act, preferably at the national level with suitable legal provisions to support the Government in 
keeping checks and controls over the private hospitals as there have been reports about the selling of 
hospital beds by them. Learning from the experience of this Pandemic, the Government should 
seriously examine it. The Act should also keep a check on the black marketing of medicines and 
product standardization. The Committee further recommends that the people should be made aware 
through awareness campaigns regarding cheaper and effective repurposed medicines to prev ent them 
from panicking and spending a huge amount of money on expensive drugs. The Committee 
recommends that good quality and affordable medicines should be provided to everyone, especially at a 
cheaper/subsidized rate to the marginalized sections of the society specially at the time of Pandemic 
like COVID-19. 
 
(Para 3.10.21 ibid)

vaccine, non-clinical data as well as complete data of Phase I, II, and III clinical trials demonstrating

may be available in near future for children of the age group of 12 to 18 years of age.

3.2.56 When asked through a questionnaire about the study conducted to assess the probable 
impact and severity of symptoms in children during the third wave. The MHA in its reply dated 21 st 
October informed that there is no specific scientific evidence either from India or globally indicating 
that children get disproportionately infected with COVID-19. Children, if infected, generally remain 
asymptomatic or exhibit mild symptoms and do not get severe disease. However, since children still 
remain susceptible to infection, Union Health Ministry has advised States on the following ongoing 
measures: 
• Union Health Ministry has advised States to undertake gap assessment of paediatric 
COVID Care facilities and upgrade health infrastructure with respect to pediatric case 
management. This includes requirement of drugs, oxygen, equipment, consumables, trained 
human resources, infection prevention, referrals, etc., if required, in collaboration with the 
private sector. 
• States/UTs have also been advised to identify and earmark designated specific areas 
for Paediatric Covid Care in all three levels of Covid facilities (COVID Care Centres; 
Dedicated COVID Health Centres and Dedicated COVID Hospitals) and including 
accompanying parents/ family members. 
• Guidelines on ‘Operationalization of COVID Care services for children and 
adolescents’ was issued and disseminated to all States/UTs on 14th June, 2021. 
• Further, with the intent to protect paediatric age group in the current and any future 
surges of cases, Guidelines for management of COVID-19 in children were also issued on 
18th June, 2021. The guideline provides guidance on the management of acute presentation 
of COVID-19 as well as Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome (MIS-C) in children and 
adolescents found temporally related to COVID-19. 
• Training modules for Paediatric essential COVID care services and communication 
strategy with messaging and information for Paediatric COVID care have been developed 
and widely circulated. 
 
3.2.57 As most paediatric cases are likely to be mild, States/UTs have been advised to undertake 
capacity building initiatives on management of COVID in the community settings using Integrated 
Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) plus approach. 
 
 
3.2.58 Regarding the cases of delta plus variant reported so far in India, the MHA informed the 
Committee that the total cases of delta plus variant reported so far in India is 83 from March till 5th 
August, 2021. However, it is a variant of concern as it is a sub-lineage of Delta variant. Hence, all 
sub- lineages of Delta variant are also classified as Variant of concern. On the basis of the data from 
the INSACOG (Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium), the trend of proportion of Delta plus 
variant vis-a-vis Delta remains < 1 percent from March to June, 2021. Data under INSACOG does not 
indicate that delta plus could escape vaccination cover. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation

Family Welfare (MoH&FW) to vaccinate people at the earliest. If need be, door to door COVID-

involvement of local level health workers, etc., to cover the entire population at the earliest. 

49

with the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization (NTAGI) and National Expert  
Group  on  Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 (NEGVAC) should assess  the requirement of

patients, in view of the observations of experts/epidemologists that a possible third wave may

Partnership building- involvement of the private sector, corporate, NGOs and other stakeholders 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.68  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the National Disaster Management Authority 
(NDMA) in combating the Corona Virus Pandemic as they have swiftly responded by building synergy  
between the Centre and States over handling the Pandemic through Standard Operating Procedures  
(SOPs), guidelines, awareness generation and most importantly, acting as a nodal centre for funding 
manpower deployment to meet exigencies. The Committee understands that this Pandemic is 
unprecedented even for the NDMA which is a dedicated body for Disaster Management. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that a separate wing may be formed in NDMA that will specialize in handling 
/managing the Pandemics like COVID-19 in the future. This wing may take a leading role in building a 
partnership of Government with the public sector, corporates, NGOs and other stakeholders. 
 
(Para 3.13.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.2.69 The observations of the Hon‟ble Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) have been noted. 
However, it is mentioned that health being the State subject, the role of Central Government is to 
provide required technical and financial assistance to States/ Union Territories (UTs) for strengthening 
of their healthcare system including management of the COVID-19 Public Health Challenge fr om time 
to time. Under the extant provisions of Disaster Management Act, 2005 the role of different institutions 
has been broadly categorized. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.70 The Committee understands that Health is a State Subject. However, COVID- 19 
Pandemic has brought the entire nation to a state of medical emergency. During such a sit uation, 
a special and well-trained dedicated workforce is required to address the mu ltifarious issues 
associated with the Pandemic. A dedicated wing of the NDMA can serve such a purpose. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation to explore the possibility of c reation of a 
separate wing in NDMA that will specialize in handling /managing the COVID-19 Pandemics like 
situation in the future. 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.71 The Committee further recommends that the measures should continuously be taken to avoid 
social stigma and fear of isolation and quarantine, by making people aware and treating them with  
respect and empathy. An interdisciplinary team of public health specialists, grassroots political and 
social leaderships and volunteers can also raise awareness about modes of transmission and methods of 
prevention of COVID-19 in the community which can be done by adopting emergency risk 
communication methods and broad-based community engagement strategies. 
(Para 3.13.8 ibid)

Action Taken

complications, so that the people suffering from various post-COVID-19 medical issues can

Health Insurance Coverage 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.75 The Committee observes that in the initial phase of Pandemic, insurance coverage was not 
given to many people who suffered from COVID-19. The private hospitals were charging exorbitantly 
high rates for the treatment of COVID patients who had to suffer a lot due to lack of any insuranc e 
coverage. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the IRDAI to create standard healt h 
insurance products and recommends that the healthcare systems need to be well prepared with well-
defined medical protocols to handle any health contingencies in future. Expanding the healthcare 
infrastructure to tier 2, 3 and 4 cities and rural areas needs focus. The Committee further recommends 
that transparency and accountability need to be increased to provide quality healthcare and to promote  
fair practices. There is a need to have regulatory oversight on all hospitals working in the c ountry to 
prevent refusal to accept insurance claims. The Committee strongly recommends that the target should 
be to make COVID-19 treatment cashless for all people that are having insurance coverage. 
(Para 3.14.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
  
3.2.76 The IRDAI has taken a number of proactive steps since the onset of Pandemic. On 4 th March, 
2020 IRDAI issued norms to all insurers for putting in place expeditious claims settlement process in 
respect of all COVID claims reported. Many insurers clarified to their policy holders about the 
availability of coverage of COVID-19 diseases. On 1 st April, 2020, public were clarified that 
indemnity-based health insurance products that cover the treatment costs of hospitalization offered by 
all general and health insurance companies cover the costs of hospitalization treatment on account of 
COVID -19. All insurers have been advised to publish FAQs on COVID-19 claims in their respective 
websites. 
 
3.2.77 In the initial stages of Pandemic, the COVID-19 treatment facility was limited to 
identified/specified Government Hospitals. However, when the permission for treatment of COVID-19 
diseases was extended to the hospitals in private sector, the policy holders availed insurance coverage 
and the actual claims started reporting to the insurers. In order to expedite   settlement of claims, the 
IRDAI vide circular dated 18 th April, 2020 fixed a turnaround time (TAT) of two hours for granting 
both cashless pre-authorization and for final discharge of the insured patient. Further in order to ensure 
that claims are settled seamlessly, all Insurers were advised to put in special efforts for electronic 
submission of documents for settlement of claims during lockdown. 
 
3.2.78 Standard COVID-19 specific health insurance products, Corona Kavach and Corona Rakshak, 
have increased awareness on health insurance and its importance besides making COVID specific 
insurance products available in the country. These initiatives were well received by public at large. 
 
3.2.79 When certain instances of private hospitals charging exorbitant rates and denying cashless 
facility to policy holders came to the notice of IRDAI, insurance companies were advised to ensure that 

53 
 
cashless facility is made available at all empanelled network providers (hospitals) and a press release is 
also issued advising the general public in the event of denial of cashless by any hospital, the concerne d 
insurance company shall be contacted for redressal of grievances.  
 
3.2.80 IRDAI also requested various State Governments, MCI and to industry bodies such as Indian 
Medical Association (IMA) and Association of Health Care Providers – India (AHPI) requesting them 
to issue appropriate instructions to facilitate cashless treatment to policyholders at private hospitals. It 
was also informed to the Dept of Financial Services that if the State Govt. / UT Admin fixes a ceiling 
on any procedure that is mandatory for all health establishments, such ceiling also needs to be adhered 
to, in case of insurance claims as well.  
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.2.81 The Committee notes that when private hospitals charged exorbitant rates and denied 
cashless facility to policyholders, insurance companies were advised by IRDAI to ensure that  
cashless facility is made available at all empanelled network providers (hospitals). Further, 
IRDAI also requested various State Governments, etc., to facilitate cashless treatment to 
policyholders at private hospitals. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the MHA  may 
take up with IRDAI to establish a system of cashless treatment for the policyholders during 
Pandemic like COVID-19 and other public health emergencies along with a regulatory ove rsight 
mechanism to put a check on the hospitals who refuse to accept insurance claims. The Committee 
would like to be apprised about the progress made in this regard.

Observation/Recommendation

3.4 Revisiting the Legislation and Key Lessons Learnt 
 
Revisiting the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, Disaster Management Act, 2005 and Inter-State 
Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1979 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.4.1 The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation mentioned at Para 4.4.10 of the Report 
and strongly recommends to revisit the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditions of Services) Act, 1979 and other relevant Labour Laws. 
(Para 6.1.9 ibid) 
Action Taken  
 
3.4.2 The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 
1979 has been subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code, 
2020 and notified on 29 th September, 2020.  In the OSH Code definition of Inter State Migrant Worker 
has been expanded in the Code on Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions to cover all 
workers, including organized, unorganized and self-employed workers. This will facilitate them to 
receive more benefits of the Government Scheme in future. 
 
3.4.3 The migrant workers are a subset of contract workers, building and other construction workers, 
self-employed workers and any other category of workers etc. They may be working in the orga nized 
and un-organized sectors or may be self-employed.  
 
3.4.4 In the OSH Code duty has been cast on every contractor or the employer, of an establi shment 
employing inter-state migrant workers in connection with the work of that establishment to ensure 
suitable conditions of work to such worker having regard to the fact that he is required to work in a 
State different from his own State. In case of fatal accident or serious bodily injury it has to be re ported 
to the specified authorities of both the States and also the next of kin of the worker. Employer has to 
extend all benefits to inter-state migrant workers which are available to a worker of that establishment 
including benefits under the Employees‟ State Insurance Act, 1948 or the Employees‟ Provident Funds 
and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 or any other law for the time being in force and the facilit y of 
medical check-up. The employer will also pay journey allowance to the migrant worker in a ye ar a 

56 
 
lump sum amount of fair for to and fro journey to his native place from the place of employment. There 
is also provision for availing benefits of Public Distribution System either in his native State or the 
destination State where he is employed. There is also provision for portability of benefits of the migrant 
workers working for the Building and Other Construction Work out of the Building and Other 
Construction Cess fund in the destination State where such migrant worker is employed. There is also a 
provision for Toll free helpline number to the inter-state migrant workers in the OSH Code. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.4.5 The Committee is of the view that given the level of education and awareness of the 
migrant workers, the benefits/facilities available to them under Occupational Safety, Health and 
Working Conditions (OSH) Code, 2020 should be widely publicized so that the intended 
beneficiaries are aware and can avail the benefits.

Impact of COVID-19 on Education 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.5.1 The Committee strongly recommends that a scheme may be worked out to provide financial 
assistance as well as low-cost subsidized devices like tablets, smartphones and computers to students

Government interventions 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
3.5.16  The Committee is aware that the country has the largest PDS network in the world, 
which is instrumental in meeting the objective of the National Food Security Act, 2013 in normal 
circumstances. However, the COVID-19 Pandemic has affected in a very harsh way, the li ves of the 
poor and the vulnerable sections of the society, both in the rural areas and in the urban areas. The 
Committee observes that during the lockdown period, due to lack of inter-operability of PDS across 
states, migrant workers were not able to take food grains from PDS shops inspite of having ration 
cards. The Committee, therefore, recommends that until One-Nation One ration card (ONOR) is 
implemented in all the States/UTs, interstate operability of ration cards should be allowed so that the 
migrant workers can take food grains from PDS shops in any State/UT. 
(Para 4.10.10 ibid) 
Action Taken

reliant for their food-security by enabling their access to the PDS foodgrains entitled under National 
Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 from any Fair Price Shop in the country using their same/existing 
ration card or Aadhaar number.

Card plan has been seamlessly enabled in 32 States/UTs covering about 69 Crore beneficiaries (86%

Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand. This Department is regularly pursuing with remaining 4 States i.e. 
Assam, Chhattisgarh, Delhi and West Bengal to implement „One Nation One Ration card‟ at the 
earliest.

4.2 Revisiting the Legislation and Key Lessons Learnt  
 
Revisiting the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, Disaster Management Act, 2005 and Inter-State 
Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1979 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
4.2.1 The Committee observes that the COVID-19 Pandemic may stay with us for a longer period. 
The response to this Pandemic has been conceived and is being guided by the provisions of the Disaster 
Management Act (NDMA), 2005 and also the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897. The Committee opines 
that the Pandemic/ epidemic fundamentally differs from disaster. Disasters happen periodically every 
year which includes floods, cyclones, train accidents, etc. whereas Pandemic/ epidemic occurs in 
decades and even once a century. The last declared Pandemic of this magnitude with huge social and 
economic fallouts was the Spanish flu of 1918. Although the provision of NDMA helped in timely 
interventions and response during the COVID-19 Pandemic, it is not meant for handling the Pandemic/  
epidemic, if it happens in future. 
(Para 6.1.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
  
4.2.2 The observations of the Hon‟ble Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) have been noted. 
 
Further Deliberations of the Committee 
 
4.2.3 In a reply to a Questionnaire, the Committee was informed by MHA that a Committee has been 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri Kamal Kishore, Member, NDMA for thorough review of 
the National Disaster Management Act, 2005. The meeting of the Committee was held on 17 th June, 
2021 and the review is under progress. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
4.2.4 The Committee notes the reply. 
 
 

63 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
4.2.5 The Committee observes that the provisions of the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, have helped in 
managing the COVID-19, but this Act is outdated as it was framed in the colonial era which was even 
well before the Spanish flu of 1918. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Epidemic Diseases 
Act, 1897 should be revisited, updated and amended so that it is fully equipped to respond to the 
challenges posed by the unanticipated onset of the Pandemic/ epidemic in the future. 
(Para 6.1.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
  
4.2.6 In light of the evolving canvas of public health globally and domestically, the need to 
strengthen public health governance, the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare intends to br ing a new 
Public Health Act.  
 
Further Deliberations of the Committee 
 
4.2.7 In its reply dated 21 st October, 2021, the Committee was informed by MHA that in order to 
effectively deal with and prevent violence against doctor’s/health  care professionals, an ordinance 
duly amending the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 was initially promulgated on April 22, 2020. 
Further it was passed by Parliament and further notified as the Epidemic Disease (Amended) Act, 
2020 on September 29, 2020. 
 
4.2.8 The amended Act provides that any act of violence against Health Care Personnel would be 
cognizable and non 
– bailable offence. Commission or abetment of such acts of violence shall be 
punishable with imprisonment of a term ranging from three months to five years and with a fine of Rs 
50,00/- to Rs. 2,00,000/-. In case of causing grievous hurt, imprisonment shall be for a term of six 
months to seven years and with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- to Rs. 5,00,000. Government has already 
constituted a Committee for review of the Disaster Management Act (DM Act) -2005. The exercise is 
at are advanced stage for finalization of the recommendations of the committee. 
 
Further Observation/Recommendation 
 
4.2.9 The Committee notes the reply.
