country. The Committee recommends that the MHA may focus first on the villages w hich 
require immediate attention or have fallen behind on development initiatives. To select 
villages, MHA may categorize villages based on sensitivity, remoteness,  cultural diversity, etc. 
For this, the MHA may take the support of Bureau of Police Resear ch & Development 
(BPR&D)  to identify such villages and their inputs may be utilized for the purpose. 
(Para 4.20.7) 
 
INTER-OPERABLE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM (ICJS) 
 The Committee notes that currently 14 States/ UTs have been integrated with ICJS 
with flow of information between police and courts, prisons, forensic and prosecution. The 
Committee recommend that the Ministry may issue advisory to the remaining States/UTs to 
implement ICJS in a specified time to strengthen criminal justice system in the country . The 
MHA may extend necessary budgetary support to the States/ UTs for the purpose. 
(Para 4.21.4) 
 
 The Committee has been given to understand that the Inter -Operable Criminal Justice 
System (ICJS) serves as a platform for data analytics for forecasting/ predicting trends in 
crimes reported region -wise, category -wise, etc. for management and control of c rimes in 
future. The Committee would like to apprised, if any, pilot study of this feature of the ICJS has 
been made in any of the States/ UTs where this system has been integrated.  
(Para 4.21.5) 
MODERNIZATION OF PRISONS 
 
 The Committee notes that the all ocation of Rs 400 crores was made in BE 2022 -23 for 
the Modernization of Prisons which was reduced to Rs 100 crores  at RE stage as funds could 
not be released due to technical  problem that arose in the wake of implementation of Central 
Nodal Agency and State Nodal Account. Further, there has been no expenditure under this 
head for FY 2022 -23 (till 31 st December, 2023). The Committee is of the opinion that this will 
delay the procurement of equipments, etc., for the prisons in the States. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the funds for the FY 2022-23 may be released to the States before 
the end of financial year. The Committee also recommends that the MHA issue advisory to the 
States and provide adequate funds for installation of jammers, door frame / hand held metal 
detectors, baggage scanners, body -worn cameras, , CCTV surveillance systems, computers, 
etc. for strengthening the security as well as to prevent inmates from using contrabands in the 
prisons. The MHA may also advise the States to arrange for appearance and trials of criminals 
from inside the prisons through video conferencing facilities within a specified time frame. 
 
 
 (Para 4.22.4) 

81 
 
 
 
 The Committee notes that in some cases, the prison staff including medical personnel of 
the prison hosp itals have been found involved in arranging mobile phones and other 
contraband items for the prison inmates. This is due to the fact that the prison staff stay posted 
in one prison for long period of time. It leads to collusion between them and the prisoners.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the MHA may advise all the States to follow rotational 
policy for transfers and postings of prison staff including medical staff and set a maximum 
tenure for which a staff can work in one prison. The MHA may c onsider creation of a cadre of 
prison staff for the Union Territories so that the personnel are transferred to different UTs 
and will not stay posted in one prison of any UT for long period of time. This along with the 
technological interventions for the s ecurity of jail cited in the Para above, will help in curbing 
the use of mobile phones and other contraband items by the criminals inside prisons. 
 
(Para 4.22.5) 
 
 
DEMAND NO. 52 TO 59 - UNION TERRITORIES 
DEMAND NO. 52 - ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS 
 
 
 The Committee is pleased to note that the UT of A&NI is currently exporting around 
44,000 metric tonnes of fish. It enjoins with the UT Administration that the export prices of 
fish per kg could be reduced by  ₹ 80 per Kg by exporting them directly from Po rt Blair to 
Bangkok. It will not only be beneficial to the country but also to the fishing business and 
fishermen as well. The Committee believes that the fisheries sector is economically crucial for 
the UT and appropriate steps should be taken to realize its full potential. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the MHA and UT Administration may take up the matter with the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation, and the Ministry of Ports. Shipping and Waterways to explore the 
possibility and initiate action for tra nsporting the harvested fish to Bangkok directly rather 
than routing it via Chennai at higher costs. It also adds that a complete plan may be developed 
for harvesting, storage, and packaging at Port Blair itself. This will also add to the 
development of business and industry there and create more employment avenues for the 
people of UT while adding to its revenues and overall development. 
(Para 5.2.6) 
 
 With regard to the funds allocated to the UT in FY 2022 -23, the Committee notes that 
only 52% of funds have been spent in the first three -quarters of the FY under the head 
"Water Supply and Sanitation”, which is an important project to improve water supply in the 
islands of the UT. The Committee recommends that the UT Administration should aspire for 
the maximum utilization of funds during a financial year. The UT Administration sho uld also 
ensure equitable utilization of funds in all quarters for the crucial projects, to prevent the rush 
of expenditure in the last quarter, and hopes that in FY 2023 -24, the situation on this count 
improves noticeably. 
(Para 5.2.7)

 The UT Administration has informed the Committee that it has started 5 electric buses 
in Swaraj Dweep Island and 14 electric buses are being procured for operating them in Port 
Blair, to promote eco-tourism. The Committee recommends that a blueprint may be prepared 
by the UT Administration for the development and promotion of eco -tourism in the Islands of 
the UT.  A feasibility study may also be conducted for the development of tourism in other 
islands of the UT, in the context of developing eco-tourism. 
 (Para 5.2.8) 
 
 The Committee notes that due to intensive development in the UT, the natural habitat 
and nesting ground of the species like Giant Leatherback Sea Turtle is being threatened. The 
Committee recommends that the MHA along with the UT Administration may take up  with 
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change of India to take appropriate 
measures for the conservation of the species in the UT which are facing the threat of 
extinction. 
(Para 5.2.9) 
  
DEMAND NO. 53 – CHANDIGARH 
 
 The Committee notes that  there are no stadiums of international level in Chandigarh 
due to which all international games are being hosted in the stadium situated in Mohali. The 
Committee recommends that the UT Administration should take the necessary steps for the 
renovation/ upgradation of Sector 16 Stadium so that international games can be hosted here. 
For this, the MHA may dedicate the necessary funds. The MHA may also take up the matter 
with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports fo r 
developing the stadiums at Sector 16 and exploring the feasibility of new buildings in this 
beautiful city. 
(Para 5.3.6) 
 
 
 The Committee takes note of the influx of population in Chandigarh which is causing 
congestion in the city. The influx is understandably related to prospects of better livelihood 
and opportunities for the poor and not -so-well population from the surrounding areas. The 
Committee recommends that the UT Administration should draw a plan whereby livelihood 
opportunities are created for this populace in the peripheral areas of the city so that the brunt 
of the influx is shifted outwards from the main areas of the city. The Committee also 
recommends that the UT Administration may take necessary steps for expansion/ upgradation 
of th e basic amenities in the periphery of the city to cater to the needs of the increasing 
population of Chandigarh.  The Committee, also, recommends that the UT Administration 
may carry out geometric improvements, construct new underpasses, and flyovers at 
appropriate places to address the problem of traffic congestion in Chandigarh. It observes that 
swift action in this regard needs to be taken otherwise by the time these measures of 
decongestion are completed the vehicular population would have increased to offset the 
facilities. 
(Para 5.3.7) 
 
 
 

83 
 
DEMAND NO. 54 - DADRA AND NAGAR HAVELI AND DAMAN AND DIU 
 
 The Committee takes note of the steps taken by the UT Administration for the 
development of tourism in Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. The Committee 
opines that the UT has a huge potential for tourism and it can become a model for eco -tourism 
in the country. It recommends that the MHA and UT Administration may take up the case 
with the Ministry of Tourism and take necessary steps for the development of various water 
sports, home stays, sea-facing hotels/ resorts, and other tourist infrastructures for holistic 
development of tourism in the UT. Efforts should be made for the creation of Tourism circuits 
in the UT which will help in showcasing all important tourist spots as well as increase 
employment and generate revenue for local people. 
(Para 5.4.5) 
 
 The Committee also recommends that adequate publicity should be given via print/ 
electronic media including social media about the tourist places of the UT. The tourism office 
of the UT should distribute printed brochures showcasing the natural beauty and lush 
greenery with captivating pictures to attract tourists. The UT Administration may collaborate 
with tour and travel companies to create tour packages and advertise the tourist attractions of 
the UT. 
(Para 5.4.6) 
 
 The Committee opines that low air connectivity to the UT is also a reason for the lack of 
development of tourism there as a lot of time of the tourists is spent travelling long distances 
by road. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Diu and Daman airports may be 
connected to more plac es which will cut the travel time and facilitate the smooth visit of 
tourists from other parts of the country. 
(Para 5.4.7) 
 
DEMAND NO. 55 –LADAKH 
 
 The Committee is of the view that considering the large area of the UT  of Ladakh, 
there is a need to stren gthen the administrative institutions and infrastructure along with the 
delegation of powers to the local administrative units in the UT of Ladakh. The Committee 
recommends that the Administration may assess the need for additional administrative posts 
in the UT and may take up with the MHA to fill up these posts for improving administrative 
outreach and public service delivery system. 
(Para 5.5.4) 
 
 The Committee notes that Leh Autonomous Hill Development Council has utilized ₹ 
500.67 (till 31st January, 2023) against the allocation of ₹ 754.53 crores at RE 2022 -23 which is 
66.35% of RE allocation. Similarly, Kargil Autonomous Hill Development Council has utilized 
₹ 568.55  crores (till 31st January, 2023) against the allocation of ₹ 756.37 crore s at RE 2022-23 
which is 75.16% of RE allocation. However, the allocation for Leh and Kargil Autonomous 
Hill Development Councils have been reduced to ₹ 334.68 crores and ₹ 333.32 crores in BE 
2023-24 respectively. The Committee would like to apprised abou t the reasons for the 
curtailment, and recommends that the budgetary allocations may be enhanced for them at the 

84 
 
RE stage. The Committee feels that devolution of financial power to the LAHDCs  will help 
them in executing their developmental projects.  
 (Para 5.5.5) 
 
 The Committee observes that the UT of Ladakh receives good insolation being situated 
at a great height. It also has good wind resources due to its valley terrain and temporal 
variation. This can be used for generating solar and wind power in th e UT. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the UT Administration may conduct a feasibility study for 
harnessing solar and wind power as well as other renewable energy sources to cater to the 
power requirement of the UT. It may rope in the Ministry of New & Renewable Energy for 
this endeavor. 
(Para 5.5.7) 
 The Committee also recommends that the UT Administration of Ladakh may take steps 
to increase green cover in Ladakh by planting more trees. This will help in generating 
employment and increase the rev enue of the local people. The MHA may extend necessary 
budgetary support and technological interventions to the UT for the same. 
(Para 5.5.8) 
 
 The Committee notes that no substantial progress has been made in the construction of the 
infrastructure of the medical college in Ladakh. The detailed project report (DPR) for the 
construction of the medical college is still  under process/examination whereas the project was 
approved in 2019.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the MHA may take up the case 
with the concerned Ministry/ Department on a priority basis to remove administrative bottlenecks 
and expedite the construction of the medical college. In the meantime, the college may commence 
its academic activities from the existing hospital of the UT so that the medical students of the UT 
can get the option of pursuing medical education in the UT. 
(Para 5.5.10) 
 
 The Committee notes that the a cquisition of small aircraft to commence flights from 
Kargil airport is in progress. The Committee understands the urgent requirement for flights 
from Kargil airport and recommends that the MHA may take up with the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation to commence commercial flights from Kargil Airport within a specified time. The 
Committee also recommends that considering the large size and difficult topography of the 
UT, the establishment of airports at Nubhra, Nyoma and Zanskar may also be ex plored to 
improve connectivity.  
(Para 5.5.12)

DEMAND NO. 57 - TRANSFERS TO DELHI 
 
 The Committee observes that the Chandrawal Water Treatment Plant  project is  
proposed to be executed in 6 packages and was expected to be completed by October, 2024. 
But due to the delay in the execution of the project, the timeline for completion has been 
revised to January, 2027. Considering the shortage of water in different parts of Delhi, the 
Committee believes that the project is vital for Delhi as it will help in providing continuous and 
equal water distribution in Delhi. The Committee, hence, recommends that the MHA may take 
up with the UT Administration of Delhi to remove the bottlenecks hampering the progress of 
the project and create a mechanism for periodic monitoring of the progress of work to ensure 
that the 6 packages of the project are executed in time and the completion date of the project is 
not revised further. 
(Para 5.7.8) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the lingering issue of land encroachment in Delhi.  The 
Committee also notes that the land demarcation in Delhi is very old. Hence, it recom mends 
that the UT Administration may consider fresh demarcation of lands in Delhi in consultation 
with all concerned stakeholders. This will help in the identification of encroached lands in 
Delhi. After the demarcation exercise is complete, a special driv e may be conducted by the UT 
Administration for removing encroachments. It should also be ensured that a grievance 
redressal mechanism may also be created to deal with the complaints of land encroachment in 
Delhi. 
(Para 5.7.9)

 The Committee notes that while ₹ 273 crores was sanctioned in BE 2022 -23, the UT 
Administration has not provided details regarding its utilization. The Committee notes the 
prgrammes undertaken by the UT Administration for conservation and restoration of the 
lake. However, it observes that  there are large number of encroachments in the Dal lake area.

pollution in the lake. The Committee observes that the visible outcome of the projects are yet

to be seen. The Committee recommends that the UT Administration may conduct fresh

 The Committee takes note of the delegation of powers to the District Development

 The Committee observes that the Ambri apple is unique to the Kashmir region and it

attractive sweet taste, crispiness, fragrant flavor, aroma, etc. for exporting these apples to the

DEMAND NO. 59 - TRANSFERS TO PUDUCHERRY 
 
 The Committee notes that t he Scheme of Special Assistance to States for Capital 
Investment with 50 years of the interest -free loan is applicable only to the States due to which 
the Union Territories with Legislature are paying the high -interest rate for the market 
borrowings. Due t o a lack of assistance from the Centre, certain important projects like the 
expansion of Puducherry Airport, the creation of infrastructure for health, education, etc. 
sectors have been affected in the UT of Puducherry. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that the MHA along with the 3 Union Territories with Legislature (Delhi, Jammu & Kashmir 
and Puducherry) may request the Ministry of Finance to consider including these 3 Union 
Territories under the Scheme. This will help these Union Territories to get int erest-free 
financial assistance for their developmental projects. The Committee hopes that the plan of 
action decided upon for the expansion of runways may be monitored by the MHA and the 
work related to the acquisition of land be completed on time. 
(Para 5.9.6)

decisions have been given by courts in 115 cases and conviction has been achieved in 
108 cases. He further informed that as on January, 2022, the sanctioned strength of 
NIA was 1,227   which has now been increas ed to 1,719 and there are around 6 50 
vacancies in the agency.

that National Forensic Science University (NFSU) has made a prototype of digital kit 
for detecting various types of narcotics including synthetic drugs.  Further, 30 zonal 
offices of NCB will be opened to cover all States of the country. He added that Anti -
Narcotics Task Force has been notified i n all th e 36 States/ UTs under Inspector-
General/ Additional Inspector-General which will further strengthen the anti -narcotics 
set up in the country. 
14. The representative of Assam Rifles informed the Committee that during 1965, 
around 65% jawans of the force were from North -Eastern States which has gradually 
reduced to 20 -22% in the present time. Further, the jawans, who belong to other 
regions of the cou ntry, are unwilling to work in North -Eastern region for a long time.

and intelligence gathering as the jawans belonging to other parts of the country are  not 
familiar with the terrain, local languages and culture of the region.

informed the Committee that they are focusing on capacity building of police 
personnel. Every year, 80 -90 thousand pers onnel are trained across domains.  Special 
trainings are being imparted to the personnel for community policing, organized 
crimes, counter-terrorism and new age crimes. There are 5 Central Detective Training 

95

and are emerging as center of excellence in police training. The representative further 
informed that BPR&D is also giving Training to Trainers  (ToT) of police personnel 
all across the country for the upcoming G20 meet.

force, they keep their capabilities at  a cutting-edge level. He added that NSG has 
excelled in anti -drone technology. They have also developed dual K9 capability by 
which dogs are being used for detection of bombs, firearms, illegal drugs as well as 
are being trained for assaults. The force is also equipping itself with requisite 
technologies to deal with Chemical , Biological, Radioactive and Nuclear (CBRN) 
threats. The force is also assessing the gaps in anti -Integrated Explosive Devices 
(IEDs) capabilities in the country.

and technological upgradation . He further informed that adequate funding has been 
provided to them for implementation of the provisions of Criminal Procedure 
(Identification) Act, 2022. The NCRB is also working to create a database of DNA, 
fingerprints, iris, etc., which will further strengthen the investigative machinery.

OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 Introduction 
 
1.1.1 North Eastern Region (NER) comprises eight States namely Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura, with a total area of almost 8 per 
cent of India. The region shares International Borders with several neighbouring countries - 
Nepal, Bhutan, China, Myanmar and Bangladesh. As per the India State of Forest Report, 2021, 
the forest resources in the North Eastern States account for 23.75% of the total forest cover of the 
country. The region is characterized by its rich bio -diversity and heavy precipitation and has 
immense potential for development.  As per Census 2011, the population of the region is about 
4.5 crores, constituting 3.78% of the total population of India. The rural population makes up 
81.64% of the total population of the region, while the urban population accounts for 18.36%.  
 
1.1.2 The Department of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was set up in 2001 to 
give focused attention to address the special needs of the NER. It was constituted, first as a 
Department in 2001 and then converted into a full -fledged Ministry in 2004 for better 
coordination between State Governments of NER and Central Mi nistries/Departments of the 
Government of India. It is the only Ministry with territorial jurisdiction. The vision of the 
Ministry is to accelerate the pace of socio -economic development of the NER so that it may 
enjoy growth parity with the rest of the co untry. For this, it coordinates with various 
Ministries/Departments primarily concerned with development activities in NER. However, 
respective Ministries/Departments remain responsible for implementing programmes in their 
respective fields.  
 
1.2 Mandates and Responsibilities of the Ministry of DoNER 
 
1.2.1 The Ministry is mandated to deal with the following matters: - 
 
(i) Matters relating to planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes and 
projects of NER including those in the sectors of Power, Irrigation, Roads and 
Communications. 
 (ii) Implementation of various schemes like Non -Lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
(NLCPR), North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS), Hill Area 
Development Programme (HADP), Schemes of NEC,  North East Road Sector 
Development Scheme (NERSDS), etc. 
(iii) Matters pertaining to various organizations under its administrative control, such as North 
Eastern Council (NEC), North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation 
Limited (NERAMAC), North Eastern Handloom and Handicrafts Development 
Corporation (NEHHDC), Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC), and North East 
Development Finance Institution (NEDFi).

1.4 Coordination with Central Ministries and Departments  
 
1.4.1 Coordinating role of the Ministry of DoNER emanates from monitoring development 
projects for socio -economic development of the NER. The Ministry coordinates with various 
Central Ministries/De partments regarding the development and welfare schemes/programmes 
they implement in the North Eastern Region. Besides, calling the progress of expenditure out of 
the earmarked outlay for NER, a set of Ministries/Departments has been assigned to senior 
officers of the Ministry for regular and continuous interactions with respective 
Ministries/Departments. Moreover, all non -exempted Ministries/ Departments have appointed 
nodal officers in their respective Ministries to coordinate over 10% GBS with the Minist ry of 
DoNER and to apprise them about the major initiatives undertaken in NER.  
 
1.4.2 In addition to the routine interactions, the Ministry also convenes sectoral review 
meetings with key Ministries such as Railways, Road Transport & Highways, Civil Aviat ion, 
Power, Environment, Forest & Climate Change, Tourism etc. for effective implementation of 
schemes and time -bound completion of major infrastructure projects in NER. Ministry of 
DoNER is represented in Inter -Ministerial Groups of major Ministries such as the Ministries of 
Road Transport and Highways ( MoRTH), Railways, Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises  
(MSME), Home, etc. and is also consulted at policy formation and project implementation stage 
through EFC/ SFC and Cabinet notes.  
 
1.4.3 The Ministry has five Inter-Ministerial Committees (IMC) viz. IMC on Roads, IMC on 
Health & Nutrition, IMC on Medicinal Aromatic Plants, IMC on HADP and IMC on STINER 
wherein issues of importance in these domains are discussed with the Stakeholder 
Ministries/Departments.

1.5 Gross Budgetary Support (GBS): Earmarking of Union Budget by Central 
Ministries/ Departments for North Eastern Region 
 
1.5.1 In October 1996, the Central Government announced ‘New initiatives for the North 
Eastern Region (NER)’, one of these measures announced was the policy decision to earmark at 
least 10% of Plan Budgets of the Central Ministries/Departments for the development of NE 
States. Accordingly, it was decided that Central Ministries/Departments, unless specifically 
exempted, will set apart 10% of their Plan Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for the NER to 
ensure a quantum jump in budgetary resource flows to the region and to fill the backlog and gaps 
in basic minimum service and infrastructure. Subsequently, allocation of funds under 10% GBS 
for the NER introduced in 2014 -15 (Statement-23), is being done annually on a lump sum basis 
by the non -exempted Central Ministries/Departments at the BE/RE stage under Major Heads 
2552 (for revenue expenditure), 4552 (for capital expen diture) and 6552 (for loan expenditure) 
under their respective functional schemes.  
 
1.5.2 In the Budget 2017 -18, several changes were introduced, e.g. dispensing with the 
distinction between Plan and Non -Plan expenditure, adoption of revenue/capital classification, 
the merger of the Railway Budget with Union Budget, discontinuation of block gra nts, etc. In 
addition, the earmarking for NER was reflected through Statement -11 of the Expenditure Profile 
of the Union Budget, as against Statement -23. To mitigate dislocation, the Ministry of DoNER 
has a special dispensation until year 2022 to carry out their schemes under Budget Head 3601.  
 
 1.5.3 As per Statement -11, a total of ₹ 68440.26 crores was allocated by 54 non -exempted 
Central Ministries/Departments for NE Region during 2021-2022 (RE), including the Ministry of 
DoNER. Similarly, for the Financial Year 2022-23, the total budgetary allocation for the NER by 
54 non-exempted Ministries/Departments is ₹ 76040.07 crores.

1.7 Central Pool of Resources for NER 
 
1.7.1 In 1997-98, when it was found that the actual expenditure of Ministries/Departments for 
NER was less than the mandatory ceiling of 10 per cent, the Government decided to create a 
"Central Resource Pool" into which the unutilized portion of the 10 per cent earmarked GBS 
would accrue at the end of the financial year.  Since 1998-99, the annual surrendered amounts 
out of the earmarked outlays of all the non -exempted Central Ministries/Departments for NER 
have been accounted as accruals to this Pool and the annual expenditure of the Ministry under 
the NLCPR scheme is bei ng accounted as withdrawal from the Pool. However, this is a notional 
pool, maintained on a proforma basis by the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry of DoNER 
monitors Ministry -wise expenditure/ surrendered amounts for the purpose of ascertaining the 
accrual to the NLCPR pool in consultation with the Ministry of Finance. 
 
INSTITUTIONS UNDER MINISTRY OF DoNER 
 
1.8 North Eastern Council (NEC) 
 
1.8.1 The North Eastern Council (NEC) was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an Act 
of Parliament under the NE C Act, 1971 (84 of 1971) marking the beginning of a new chapter of 
concerted and planned endeavour for rapid socio -economic development of the North Easter n 
Region (NER). Over the last 48 years, the Council has played a significant role in ushering 
development into the Region at a time when most States were in their formative stages. Road and 
air connectivity were supported, foundations for important regional Institutions were established, 
and various socio -economic infrastructures were created across the length and breadth of the 
Region, making a difference in the lives of the people and thereby earning goodwill in the local 
community. Presently, NEC is looking to continue its efforts, especially in terms of gap-filling in 
areas which have escaped the attention of various development agencies and creating 
convergence at different levels. NEC is also looking at building capacities, sharing best practices 
and introducing cutting-edge technologies among the NE States.

1.9.1 Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC) now re -named as North East Cane and 
Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) is an ISO 9001:20 08 certified organization and was 
established in the year 2000 as part of Cane and Bamboo Technological Upgradation and

Department of Science & Technology (DST), Govt. of India and United Nations Industrial

1.10 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited  
(NEHHDC) 
 
1.10.1 The North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Ltd 
(NEHHDC) was established in the year 1977 at Shillong, Meghalaya with the mandate of 
promotion and development of Handlooms and Handicrafts Sector in the North Eastern Region. 
NEHHDC h as been providing marketing support through procurement of Handicrafts and 
Handlooms products directly from the Artisans, Weavers and Self -Help Groups at clusters and 
selling the same through its Sales Emporia located at Shillong, Guwahati, Kolkata, New De lhi 
and Gujarat and through Sales Promotion Offices located at Chennai and Bangalore and also 
through the conduct of various exhibitions and marketing events all over the country. 
 
1.11 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited  
(NERAMAC)  
 
1.11.1 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) Limited was 
incorporated in 1982 as a Central Public Sector Enterprise under the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER). NERAMAC has been envisaged 
and is functioning as not just a marketing agency for farmers and entrepreneurs, but also 
undertakes agri-horti projects, skill curriculum supplies inputs, GI produ ces promotion activities, 
agri-events and assists in setting up of horticulture value chain (food processing) etc. to approach 
the aspect of Agri -Horti development holistically. A revival package for NERAMAC was 
approved in August 2021. The Corporation is on track to achieve a turnover target of ₹ 64 crores 
set at the time of approval.

1.12 North Eastern Region Community Resource Management Society (NERCRMS) 
 
1.12.1 The North Eastern Region Community Resource Management Society (NERCRMS) is a 
society under the North Eastern Council (NEC), Ministry of DoNER, Government of India for 
the implementation of development projects in the North Eastern Region of India. The Soc iety 
successfully implemented 3 (three) phases of the NERCORMP project  i.e. (a) NERCORMP -I 
from 1999 to 2008 jointly funded by Govt. of India and IFAD’ (b) NERCORMP -II from 2010 to 
2017 jointly funded by Govt. of India and IFAD and (c) NERCORMP -III from 2 014 to 2021 
with funding from Govt. of India only.  
 
1.12.2 The NERCORMP-I & II was implemented in 6 districts in States i.e. Karbi Anglong and  
Dima Hasao districts of Assam; Ukhrul and Senapati districts of Manipur;  West Garo Hills and 
West Khasi Hills districts of Meghalaya. The NERCORMP -III was implemented in Changlang 

7 
 
and Tirap (including Logding) districts of Arunachal Pradesh, Chandel and Churachandpur 
districts of Manipur. The society developed community -based institutions for implementation of 
NERCORMP-I, II & III.  During three phases of NERCORMP , the society formed 2889 Natural 
Resource Management Groups (NaRM -Gs), 8403 Self Help Groups (SHGs), 290 NaRM -G 
Cluster Associations, 300 SHG Federations, 4 Community -Based Micro Credit Institutions and 
50 Farmer Producer Groups. A total 1,18,843 Household in 2532 villages benefited from 
NERCORMP I, II & III with a total cost to Govt. of India ₹ 731.28 crores (Total investment 
including funds from other agencies, support from financial institutions and com munity 
contribution was ₹ 970.94 crores).  
 
1.12.3 The NERCRMS continue implementing development interventions beyond NERCORMP 
covering all 8 (eight) States of NER of India with sanction/allotment of additional 
projects/schemes of North Eastern Council beyond 2021. 
 
1.13 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi) 
 
1.13.1 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd (NEDFi) is a public limited 
company established in 1995 under the Companies Act 1956. It is notified as a Public Financial 
Institution under Section 4A of the said Act and is registered as a Non -Banking Financial 
Company (NBFC) in 2002 with RBI. The core business of the Corporation comprises lending 
activities (fund -based) and fee -based activities. The lending activities are u ndertaken through  
project finance schemes and microfinance schemes. The Corporation also provides fee -based 
Advisory & Consultancy Services to the Central and State Governments. 
 
1.13.2 NEDFi has been playing an important role in facilitating the setting u p of new industrial 
and service sector projects in the North Eastern States. During 1st January to 31 st December, 
2022, NEDFi extended financial assistance to 3263 projects with total sanctions & disbursements 
of ₹  1035.34 crores and ₹  725.34 crores respectively, facilitating the capital formation of ₹  
2119.64 crores. Various sectors financed were hotels & tourism, healthcare, education & training 
institute, food processing, handlooms & handicrafts, microfinance etc.  
 
1.14 Science & Technology Intervention North Eastern Region (STINER) 
 
1.14.1 Ministry of DoNER with the close collaboration of the office of the Principal Scientific 
Adviser (PSA) to the Government of India initiated STINER ( Science & Technology 
Interventions in the North East Region ) in 2017 -18 as a mechanism for synergy between 
technology and users. STINER supports appropriate technology dissemination of field -tested 
technologies from S&T institutions to the farmers /artisans of NER which helps augment 
economic development/livelihood in the NER. The STINER Project was officially transferred to 
North Eastern Council, Shillong from Ministry along with a budget Provision of ₹ 40 crores in 
June, 2016 for sanctioning funds to implement the project by CSIR -NEIST, Jorhat. STINER has 
been proposed to be implemented in Hub & Spoke mode, where STINER-hub is started at CSIR-
NEIST, Jorhat and a STINER -spoke is to be established at every North E astern States. Already, 
STINER-Spoke at SASARD, Nagaland has been established and six other STINER spoke s 
projects for the State of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Manipur, Tripura and Sikkim 
have been submitted, presented, reviewed and waiting for final approval.

long-term planning regarding the funds that could be spent in three or five years was not 
possible. However, in January, 2023, with the approval of the Ministry of Finance, all the 
schemes of the Ministry were approved by the Cabinet till 2025 -26. Now, they are approved up

Observation/ Recommendation 
 
2.2.4 The Committee is pleased to note that all the schemes of the Ministry have been 
approved up to the limit of 2025 -26 and feels that the additional time of 3 years available 
with the Ministry of DoNER may be enough to plan and execute its schemes. The 
Committee hopes that funds under the schemes can now be spent with proper planning and 
recommends that the Ministry prepare a road map in consultation with all stakeholders for 
the time-bound implementation of schemes considering the budgetary allocation availab le 
to them. The Committee further notes that the road sector schemes under Non -Lapsable 
Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR), Hill Area Development Programme (HADP) and 
North East Road Sector Development Scheme ( NERSDS) have been merged under one 
head of the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) -Roads 
component. This will allow the Ministry to use the allocated amount of ₹ 2491.00 crores to 
prioritize their investments. Significant progress has been made in developing roadways in 
the NER during the last couple of years. The Committee hopes that this merger of schemes

2.3.5 The Committee was informed that there has been a substantial change in the way of  
allocation and spending of funds in the FY 2022 -23. Previously, the funds were released to the 
States or their working institutions in advance installments from the budget al location and were 
considered as expenditure. This used to lead to actual spending later, which the Ministry used to 
know through certificates after utilization. The next time, funds were again sanctioned in advance. 
Further, funds were released via Treasury to State Governments / Implementing Agencies (IAs). 
According to the revised procedure for the flow of funds implemented in accordance with the 
Department of Economic Affairs OM dated March 9, 2022, funds are released to Implementing 
Agencies (IAs) by CNA against submitted bills for work done by IA s. Now, funds  can only be 
released to an IA after they submit a “Zero Balance Certificate”. The Committee was also 
informed that NEDFi has been selected as the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) by the Ministry o f 
DoNER and has opened scheme-wise accounts for implementing the said guidelines.  
 
2.3.6 The Committee was informed that since this was the first year of the implementation of the 
new system, the Ministry had to decide whether the funds released earlier to the States or their 
working institutions as advances were still unspent  or for which a  utilization certificate ha d not 
been given.  So, either a utilization certificate is to be given to confirm that the funds have been 
spent or to be returned to the scheme -wise accounts created by the CNA. This process is going on 
right now. It was further informed that the unspent balances availab le with the State 
Governments/Implementing Agencies were required to be returned to CNA Accounts.  
 
2.3.7 According to Ministry’s provisional estimate, as of April 1, 2022, States had about ₹ 3,200 
crores against donor schemes whose utilization certificate s had not been received, and it was not 
known whether they were spent or not. Further, out of this amount of about ₹ 3,200 crores, 
utilization certificates worth about ₹ 1,900 crores have been given by the States that this amount 
has been spent, and about ₹ 800 crores have been deposited in CNA accounts. They will be made 
available to them again when they spend in the future. For the remaining ₹ 500 crores, some States 
are still returning or giving utilization certificates. For this, the deadline for this year has been set 
as March, 2023. The Ministry is in constant touch with them and monitoring this. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
2.3.8 The Committee notes that, in accordance with the Department of Economic Affairs' 
directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes 
has been implemented. The Committee also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize 
around 16% of the allocated amount in the first three quarters of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination 
mechanism with the NEC, States and implementing agencies so that such a situation , that 
arose in the Financial Year 2022-23, can be addressed promptly and without delay in order 
to maximize the utilization of funds.  The Committee also recommends that the Ministry 
make all-out efforts to ensure that the balance of ₹  500 crores is accounted for by the close 
of the financial year 2022-23.

3.1 Schemes of North East Council  
 
3.1.1 The North Eastern Council, which was constituted as a statutory advisory body by an Act 
of Parliament under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971 (Act No. 84 of 1971) , works under the 
administrative control of the Ministry of DoNER. It provides financial assistance for various 
projects, including infrastructure projects like the construction of roads, improving air 
connectivity, etc., through State Governments.   
 
3.1.2 The "Schemes of the NEC" is a Central Sector Scheme with a 100% Grant from the 
Government of India. The projects under the scheme are implemented in focused areas through 
designated agencies of the States/Central Government with a stipulation that in the case of State 
agencies, the funds will be transferred to implementing agencies.  
 
3.1.3 The Committee was informed that the Union Cabinet, in its meeting held in January 
2020, approved earmarking of 30 per cent of the North E astern Council's (NEC's) allocation for 
new projects under the existing "Schemes of North Eastern Council" for focused development of 
deprived areas; deprived/neglected sections of society and emerging priority sectors in the North 
Eastern States. The bala nce allocation shall be bifurcated into the existing two components viz. 
State component-60 per cent and Central component-40 per cent.

monitoring of development schemes and projects in the North Easter n Region, should

3.2 Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim /North East Special 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
 
3.2.1 The Scheme of ‘Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim’ is conventionally 
also called the Non Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) Scheme. NLCPR Scheme 
aims to fill the gap in the infrastructure sector of the North Eastern Region by providing financial 
assistance to the projects prioritized by the Central and State Government. The Ministry gets 
annual budgetary allocation for funding projects under NLCPR Scheme. Funding of projects 
under the NLCPR scheme is on a 90:10 sharing pattern betwe en Central and State Governments. 
In view of the restructuring of the Scheme, no new projects are being sanctioned under the 
Scheme, and only ongoing projects are being funded. 
 
3.2.2 The NLCPR scheme was replaced by the North Eastern Special Infrastructur e 
Development Scheme (NESIDS) which came into force on 15 th December, 2017 in place of the 
NLCPR-State scheme. It is a Central Sector Scheme with 100% central funding under which 
financial assistance to NER States is provided to fill up the gaps in specified sectors of :- 
 
(a) physical infrastructure relating to water supply, power and connectivity to enhance 
tourism and  
(b) social sectors for the creation of infrastructure in the areas of primary and secondary 
sectors of education and health.

CHAPTER – IV 
 
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
 
4.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors  
 
4.1.1 The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the Department of Agriculture and 
Farmers welfare ( DA&FW) is organized into 28 Divisions for coordination with State-level 
agencies and implementation of schemes in their respective fields. Further, one Public Sector 
Undertakings (National Seeds Corporation), nine autonomous bodies including Small Farmers’ 
Agri Business Consortium, National Horticulture Board, Natio nal Centre for Cold Chain 
Development etc., ten national level cooperative organizations and two authorities are 
functioning under the administrative control of the Department. Most of the central sector’s 
schemes related to Agriculture are implemented by DA&FW including Agriculture Infrastructure 
Fund, Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc.       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
4.1.2 The major Schemes implemented by DA&FW to develop agriculture and farmers’ 
welfare in NER include:  
 
a) Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi  
The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM Kisan) is a central sector scheme under 
which financial support o f ₹ 6,000 per year in three equal instalments is transferred directly into 
the bank accounts of eligible farmers under Direct Benefit Transfer. The scheme became 
operational in December 2018. Under the scheme, State Government and UT administration 
identify the farmer families which are eligible for financial support as per the scheme guidelines.  
 
b) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana 
The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides insurance coverage and 
financial support to the farmers in the event of fa ilure of any of the notified crops due to natural 
calamities, pests & diseases. The scheme also encourages farmers to adopt innovative and 
modern agricultural practices and stabilizes the income of farmers to ensure their continuance in 
farming activity. T he scheme is implemented by a multiagency framework by a few selected 
insurance companies under the supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare 
(MoA&FW), Govt of India. 
 
c) Agriculture Infrastructure Fund 
The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund ( AIF) is a central sector scheme to facilitate the 
financing of agricultural infrastructure at the post -harvest stage i.e., farm gates and aggregation 
points.  The scheme was launched in 2020 and has a total outlay of ₹ 1 Lac crore. The scheme 
provides Interest subvention of 3% p.a., limited to ₹ 2 crores per project in one location, though 
the loan amount can be higher. The scheme also has a cap on lending rate, so that benefit of 
interest subsidy reaches the beneficiary and services to farmers remain affordable. 
 
d) Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North – Eastern Region 
The Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eas tern Region 
(MOVCDNER) is a sub mission under National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). It 
is a central sector scheme and aims at the development of certified organic production in a value 

31 
 
chain mode to link growers with consumers and to support the development of the entire value 
chain starting from inputs, seeds, and certification, to the creation of facilities for collection, 
aggregation, processing marketing and brand building initiative. 
 
e) Modified Interest Subvention Scheme 
The Government implements a modified interest subvention scheme to ensure that 
nominal interest rates are charged to farmers for short -term crop loans for agriculture and allied 
sectors. Under the scheme for FY 2021 -22, the lending rate to farmers and the rate of interest 
subvention has been kept at 7% and 2% respectively.  
 
f) Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana - Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and 
Allied Sector Rejuvenation 
The scheme was originally initiated as RKVY in 2007 to ensure the holistic development 
of agriculture and allied sectors by allowing States to choose their own agriculture and allied 
sector activities as per the State Agriculture Plan. It is a central sponsored scheme with a funding 
pattern ratio of 60:40 between the Centre and States and 90:10 for North Eastern States and 
Himalayan States. RKVY -RAFTAAR aims to make farming a remunerative economic activity 
through the strength ening of farmer’s efforts, promoting Agri -business entrepreneurship, focus 
on pre & post-harvest infrastructure.  
 
g) Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture 
Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme for the holistic growth of the horticulture sector covering fruits, vegetables, root & tuber 
crops, mushrooms, spices, flowers, aromatic plants, coconut, cashew, cocoa, and bamboo. Under 
MIDH, the Government of India (GOI) contributes 60% of the total outl ay for developmental 
programmes in all the States except States in North East and the Himalayas, 40% share is 
contributed by State Governments.  
 
4.1.3 The Committee, in its meeting held on 27th February, 2023, discussed about various 
indigenous crop varieties in the NER. The Committee discussed about Boka Saul; an indigenous 
variety of rice produced exclusively in lower regions of Assam. It was discussed that this rice is 
not cooked conventional ly, as it can be soaked in warm or cold water, and after around 30 -40 
minutes, it is ready for consumption. It does not need any kind of fuel to cook. The Committee 
believes that the potential of this variety of rice can be tapped as it is not only nutriti ous but can 
be used as an alternate source of food in emergencies like flood, earthquake and disaster 
management. It could also be used for army and armed forces personnel posted in high altitude 
or remote areas.  
 
4.1.4 Further, the abundance of Bamboo in  NER and the viability of bamboo for commercial 
purpose was also discussed in the meeting of the Committee. Bamboo is not covered in the 
category of a tree after the amendment made to Indian Forest Act, 1927, and there is no 
prohibition on growing or cutti ng bamboo even outside the forest areas. This makes it easier to 
use Bamboo commercially. 
 
 
 
 

32 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.1.5 Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue their farming activities 
through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upli ftment of the farmers in North Eastern 
Region.  The Committee appreciates the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
which is providing insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in the event of 
failure of any notified crops due to natural c alamities, pest and diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum be nefits are reaped out of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 
4.1.6 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be given and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 
4.1.7 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been  fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute ( IPIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 
4.1.8 The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such as beetl e nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country. 
 
4.2 Organic Farming in NER

This can be best utilized by promoting tourism in NER. Every State in the North East has 
its own language, food, and cultural practices, which are beautifully represented through 
annual festivals such as the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland, the Sangai Festival of Manip ur,

preserving the autonomy of these tribal areas. The Committee re commends that the

4.9 Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
 
4.9.1 The Committee inquired about the status of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport 
(KMMTT). The Ministry informed the Committee that KMMTT, a strategic connectivity project 
to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar has two components: (i) Waterways 
component and (ii) Roadways component. 
(I)       Waterways component: The construction of port and inland water transport was 
completed in December 2018. All works for the operationalization of the port have been 
  completed. Sittwe port is now ready for operationalization. A trial run from Sittwe port 
(Myanmar) was conducted successfully on 13 January, 2023.  
(II)      Road component: The Road component of KMMTT includes a new green field road 
project of 109.2 km to be built from Paletwa in Myanmar to Zorinpui on the India -Myanmar 
border (Mizoram) to double -lane NH specifications. The work was earlier awarded to the Joint 
Venture (JV) of Engineers Projects (India) Limited and C&C Construction Co.  Ltd. in 2017. 
However, due to slow progress and the bankruptcy of the lead partner of JV, the contract was 
terminated. Now IRCON International has been appointed as the New Project Executing agency 
for the execution of the project. The agreement with IRCO N has been signed on 7 th March 2022. 
IRCON has awarded the contract for 40 km stretch from Paletwa end (Myanmar) i.e. 0 km –40 
km and for 99 km –109 km (from Zorinpui end). Work has started in 0 km –10 km section (i.e 
from Paletwa, Myanmar end). Surveying and site cleaning works have started in km 10 - km 40 
section (Myanmar end) and 99 km –109 km (Zorinpui, Mizoram end). 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.9.2 The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the 
waterways component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a 
strategic connectivity project to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all 
the works that have been done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes 
and hopes that since a new  Project Executing Agency has been appointed for execution of 
the road component of KMMTT, similar commitment may be shown to realise the 
completion of road component of the project in a time bound manner.

directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes

mechanism with the NEC, States and implementing agencies so that such a situation, that

SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
  
Agriculture and Allied Sectors  
 
Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue  their farming activities 
through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upliftment of the farme rs in North Eastern 
Region.  The Committee appreciates the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
which is providing insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in the event of 
failure of any notified crops due to natural calamities, pest and  diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum benefits are reaped o ut of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 (Para 4.1.5) 
 
 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be gi ven and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 (Para 4.1.6) 
 
 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute (I PIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 (Para 4.1.7) 
 
The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such a s beetle nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country. 
  (Para 4.1.8)

since 2022-23; major  changes in methodology of expenditure in the financial year 
2022-23; monitoring expenditure of earmarked funds (10% Gross Budgetary 
Support) by non-exempted Ministries/Departments; Resource augmentation for NE 
– 10% GBS spent in N orth Eastern Region ;  achievements of North Eastern 
Council, new schemes of the Ministry,  Prime Minister’s Development initiatives 
for North East Region (PMDevINE)  which replaced the earlier scheme  for road 
development in the North East ern Region; list of selected 11 Projects under PM -
DevINE; achievements made in PMDevINE  scheme; various projects undertaken 
for connectivity of the North Eastern States for promotion of trade ; rail link from 
Agarthala to Akhaura via Bangladesh; efforts made for enhancing private funding 
in the north east ern region for infrastructure  development; other a ctivities of 
Primary Livelihood Sector; development across different i nfrastructure Ministries;  
etc. 
4. The Chairman and Members of the Committee raised s everal queries 
pertaining to allocation  and utilization of funds by the line Mi nistries during the 
last ten years;  reasons for delay in works on  Agarthala to Akhaura rail link and 
Pukhungri-Avanku-Layshi Road ; reasons for delay in settlement of water 
distribution of Feni river with Bangladesh;  reasons for under utilization of funds  
for development of infrastructure in North Eastern Region; reasons for switching 
over to new methodology for disbursement of funds;  status on utilization of funds 
allocated under the Central schemes made available through online mode; status on 

59 
 
financial discipline in fund utilization in Ministry of DoNER and the percentage of 
the funds spent during the last three months of the financial year; etc. 
5. The Chairman and Members of the Committee made some suggestions that 
inter-alia included efforts to be ma de for completion  of remaining portion of 
Agartala-Akhura rail link project for providing cross -border rail linkage between 
India and Bangladesh for development of North Eastern Region of India; initiatives 
to be taken at the level of higher authorities to  minimize the hurdles in completion 
of projects/schemes; ensuring uniform fund utilization during the financial year; 
timeline  to be decided for completion of project; use of bio fertilizers to increase 
agriculture production; efforts to be made for exploring commercial viability of 
bamboo and other crops in North Eastern Region; etc.  
6. The Secretary, Ministry of DoNER and other concerned officers replied to 
some of the queries raised by the Members.  On other queries, the Ministry was 
asked to furnish written replies to the Secretariat within three days.

1 
 
Report 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the 
Ministry of Home Affairs on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Thirty 
Seventh Report of the Committee on Police - Training, Modernisation and Reforms. The Two 
Hundred Thirty Seventh Report was presented to the Rajya Sabha /laid on the Table of Lok 
Sabha, on 10th February, 2022. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of Home Affairs in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Thirty Seventh Report have been 
categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos. 1.4.8, 2.2.19, 2.7.4, 2.7.6, 2.11.3, 3.12.4, 3.17.4, 3.27.3, 4.3.3, 
4.4.4, 4.5.5, 4.10.7, 4.16.4 (of Two Hundred Thirty Seventh Report) 
Total recommendations- 13 Accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted 13 of its 
recommendations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
 
Chapter II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 2.2.15, 2.2.16, 2.2.17, 2.2.18, 
2.5.2, 2.6.4, 2.6.5, 2.7.5, 2.8.3, 2.8.4, 2.9.6, 2.9.7, 2.10.4, 2.10.5, 2.12.2, 2.13.3, 2.13.4, 
2.14.10, 2.14.12, 3.15.2, 3.15.3, 3.16.8, 3.17.3, 3.19.6, 3.19.7, 3.20.3, 3.20.4, 3.21.12, 
3.21.13, 3.25.2, 3.26.4, 4.6.12, 4.8.4, 4.9.5, 4.12.5, 4.13.9, 4.16.5,4.17.7, 4.18.2 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 39 Not to be pursued further. 
 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry in 
respect of 39 recommendations and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations 
further. 
 
Chapter III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee is 
not satisfied with the replies of the Ministry: Para Nos. 2.2.20, 3.21.9, 3.21.10, 3.21.11, 
3.24.8, 3.27.4, 4.7.8, 4.17.8 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 8 Not convincing replies. 
 
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of 8 of its 
recommendations contained in Chapter III and desires that the Ministry should take further 
necessary action and furnish convincing replies in respect of those recommendations within a 
time frame of three months after the presentation of the Report.  
 
Chapter IV: The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government have not been received: Para Nos. 1.4.4, 2.3.6, 2.4.2, 2.9.8, 3.16.7, 3.17.5, 
3.18.5, 3.22.5, 3.22.6,  3.23.5, 3.24.7, 4.4.5, 4.6.9, 4.6.10,  4.6.11, 4.9.4, 4.11.5, 4.13.8, (ibid) 
Total Recommendations –18 To be pursued further. 
 
In respect of the 18 recommendations placed in Chapter IV, the Committee feels that 
the Ministry has either furnished interim replies or couched its response in vague terms. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry furnish pointed and detailed Action Taken Notes in 
respect of the recommendations categorized in Chapter IV as per the intention and spirit of 
the recommendations of the Committee within three months. 
 
 As per the categorisation indicated above, the para-wise details of the ATNs are being 
discussed in the succeeding Chapters. 
 
 

 
2 
 
CHAPTER- I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Ranking of Police Stations 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.1.1 The Committee appreciates the initiative of ranking of police stations in the country. 
The Committee believes that the annual ranking of police stations work as a constant guide 
for improvements. It also provides a picture of the state of physical infrastructure, resources 
and deficiencies at the level of police stations. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the MHA may incentivize the best police stations in terms of funds and resources. It will 
recognize their hard work and create an environment of healthy competition among all police 
stations in the country.  
(Para 1.4.8 of 237th  Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 The Annual Assessment of the Best Police Stations Scheme was undertaken since 
Year- 2017 to identify and recognize the ten best police stations of the country and also the 
best police station in a particular State or Union Territory.  
1.1.3 Report in this regard is released in the DsGP-IsGP Conference every year. There are 
two sets of awards given to police stations. The 3 best police stations selected for that year 
will be awarded ‘Shield’. Further, the top 10 police stations of the country and the top police 
stations of each State/UTs have been given certificates.  
1.1.4 Further, under the umbrella scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces, approved in 
September 2017, a component of “incentives for police reforms” was included in the 
implementation structure of the scheme of “Assistance to States for Modernisation of 
Police”.  It was decided to earmark a certain amount each year for awarding incentives to 
the State Government for the implementation of Police Reforms. To incentivize the 
implementation of police reforms as recommended by various committees, originally a 
provision of keeping up to 10% of the total annual allocation of the scheme was made.  This 
incentive fund has been increased to ‘up to 20%’ from the year 2019-20. 
Further Recommendation  
1.1.5 The Committee notes the reply.  
1.2 Training Mandate of Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1  With regard to the training syllabi of the Academies, the Committee is of the firm 
opinion that the training syllabus should be dynamic and in sync with the changing need and 
times. A static syllabus will only make the entire training process redundant and a mere 
formality. The Committee notes that SVPNPA and NEPA do review the content of the 
training curriculum from time to time. However, the Committee recommends that a 
mechanism may be developed to review and update the training curriculum biennially/ 
triennially based on the professional requirement and ground-level assessment of the POs. 
(Para 2.2.19 ibid) 

 
3 
 
Action Taken  
 
 Action Taken Report from SVPNPA:- 
 
1.2.2 Regular review of syllabus and teaching methodology takes place. Academy also has 
high-level Academy Boards comprising senior civil/police officers, eminent educationists etc., 
as its members. The Board is headed by the Union Home Secretary. The Board periodically 
(once in three years) reviews inter-alia the syllabi and training methodology of various 
courses conducted in the Academy. 
 
1.2.3 On the basis of recommendations of the 37th Board meeting and the 39th Board 
meeting of SVPNPA Board, the Academy conducted a comprehensive Training Needs 
Analysis (TNA) in the year 2020. It is proposed to conduct the TNA exercise once every five 
years. 
 
1.2.4 For all the Mid-Career Training Programme (MCTP) Course guiding principle for 
the design of the course is the recommendations of Dr. Trinath Mishra, IPS (Retd.) 
Committee Report. 
 
1.2.5 However, as recommended by Hon’ble Committee that “a mechanism may be 
developed review and update the training curriculum biennially triennially based on the 
professional requirement and ground level assessment of the POs” will be ensured. 
 
1.2.6 These recommendations will be given due importance while designing the next MCTP 
Course. Contemporary topics like the Dark Net, Crypto Currencies, Drones, Big Data 
Analytics & use of Technology for better policing have been made an integral part of the 
Course Design. 
 
 Action Taken Report from NEPA :- 
 
1.2.7 NEPA is making constant efforts to keep abreast with the evolving challenges in the 
field of policing. All modern topics related to policing are incorporated in the syllabus, as 
and when required. In addition, eminent resource personnel from respective fields from all 
over the country, are invited to enlighten the trainees on the trending topics. 
 
1.2.8 In a bid to further improve training, North Eastern Police Academy (NEPA) is 
conducting a Training Needs Analysis, wherein its faculty officers are deputed to member 
states to get a first-hand impression of the training requirements and also obtain suggestions 
from supervisory officers vis-à-vis their specific needs. NEPA will ensure to keep up the 
recommendations of the committee. 
 
Further recommendation  
1.2.9 The Committee notes the commitment of the SVPNPA to develop a mechanism 
to review and update the training curriculum biennially/ triennially based on the 
professional requirement and ground-level assessment of the POs and designing the 
next Mid-Career Training Programme (MCTP) Course as per the recommendation of 
the Committee. The Committee further recommends that the training curriculum for 
the personnel should be developed in a hybrid mode – a mix of online and offline 
modules. 
 
 

 
4 
 
1.3 Training on Arrest and Interrogation Techniques 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.3.1 The Committee recommends that the MHA may advise States/UTs to impart adequate 
training to the police personnel on the procedure during arrests. The training should also 
emphasize that the rights of the detainee are not violated by resorting to manhandling during 
arrests. The police personnel should also be trained to understand  that their role is not just to 
arrest people but also to protect people and deter crime.  
(Para 2.7.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 The Advanced Course on Investigation and Detection of Crime (10 Weeks) includes 
sessions on Arrest and related topics (A part of a module on Law, Police Procedure and 
Report Writing) (4 days). 
1.3.3 The subjects covered are: 
• Arrest – (D.K. Basu Vs. State of West Bengal) Remand prayer 
• Hand cuffing 
• Test Identification (TI) Parade 
• Bail 
• Legal Provision. 
1.3.4 Further, BPR&D is regularly conducting webinar, symposium, conference etc. with 
stakeholders which include officers from State Government. 
Further Recommendation  
1.3.5 The Committee notes the reply.    
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.6 The Committee also recommends that the MHA may advise States to sensitize the 
investigating officers to use relevant provisions under the penal laws while registering a case 
and precautions be taken during trial to secure conviction. 
(Para 2.7.6  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.7 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/UT 
Administrations to maintain law and order, including investigation, registration and 
prosecution of crimes, protection of life and property, etc. Police Forces of the States work 
within the existing legal and institutional framework. 
 
 
 

 
5 
 
Further Recommendation  
1.3.8 The Committee notes that due to lack of knowledge of procedure among ground 
level police personnel, unknowingly, loopholes are generated in the process of 
investigation, collection of evidence, filing of charge-sheets which are taken advantage 
by the culprits.  This leads to State prosecution losing a lot of cases in the courts.  This is 
a undeniable fact in respect of all States/UTs.  Hence, the Committee desires that while 
centre may refrain from involving in day to day administrative matters of police   
enforcement of law and order, it ought to device a mechanism by making/amending the 
existing provisions suitably so that the training of police personnel from the level of 
constable to the level of SHO by States/UTs can be standardized so far as procedure on 
inter-state registration of cases and prosecution of crimes is concerned.  The Committee 
believes this could strengthen the law and orders system in the country to prevent 
criminals operating inter-state and taking advantage of loopholes to escape prosecution  
 
1.4 Creation of Dedicated Reserve Training Pool 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that most of the time, police stations are understaffed, and 
when the officials are summoned for training, they don’t get relieved on time. As a result, if 
the training slot is for 100 constables, only 50 to 60 percent of the constables are allowed to 
take training. Therefore, the Committee recommends that MHA may advise States/UTs for 
creation of a reserved training pool at the District level so that if training is proposed to be 
given to 100 constables, then those chosen for training could be replaced with reserve 
constables from the training pool created for the purpose and there is no hesitancy on the part 
of the higher police officers in sending the personnel for training. 
(Para 2.11.3  ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4.2 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India.  It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments to fill up the 
vacancies in the police force in their respective States.   The Centre also issues advisories 
from time to time to the States for filling up these vacancies in the States and to bring in the 
requisite reforms in the police administration to meet the lawful expectations of the people. In 
case the vacant posts of police personnel are filled by the States/UTs, the reserved training 
pool will automatically be created in a comprehensive manner.  
Further Recommendation  
1.4.3 The Committee notes the reply.  
1.5 Scheme for Modernisation of State Police Forces 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5.1  The Committee appreciates the component of “incentives for police reforms” under 
the scheme of “Assistance to States for Modernisation of Police”.  The Committee notes that 
the incentive fund has been increased to up to 20% from the year 2019-20. The Committee 
however opines that the progress in police reforms has been slow and hopes that the 
incentives given to better performing States for taking various measures on police reforms 

 
6 
 
will encourage other States to fast-track the efforts towards modernisation of their police. The 
Committee recommends that the MHA may put the information in public domain about the 
States that are leading and lagging in the modernisation process.  This will create a sense of 
competition and put pressure on the States lagging behind to perform better. The Committee 
also observes that the issues behind the under-utilization of funds by the States also need to 
be identified. Therefore, the Committee also recommends that the MHA should consider 
constituting a Committee which can visit the underperforming States and 
assist/advise/persuade them to utilize the funds in a planned manner; otherwise the situation 
in these states may take a long time to show improvements. 
(Para  3.12.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.5.2 The information about the States that are leading in utilizing funds and taking 
maximum benefit of the scheme of ‘Assistance to States for Modernisation of Police’ has been 
published in the Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2020-21.   
1.5.3  In so far as recommendations regarding the visit of officers to identify and resolve 
issues behind the under-utilization of funds by the States is concerned; stipulation is being 
made in the guidelines of the scheme so that the same can be institutionalized. Besides that, 
the Ministry issues reminders to the States and implementation is reviewed regularly through 
Review Meetings. Further, the ‘High Power Committee’, which approves Action Plans under 
the scheme also discusses issues related to the under-utilization of funds with the 
representatives of the State Government and State Police. 
Further Recommendation  
1.5.4 The Committee notes the reply.   
1.6 Use of Technology by State Police 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.6.1 The Committee observes that technology like artificial intelligence, big data, etc. can 
effectively help in mapping the crime hotspots and getting a digital footprint of the criminals. 
This can be used to deploy force more effectively thereby reducing/preventing crime. 
Artificial intelligence can be used to draw correlations between the types of crime, time, 
location, match fingerprints, facial images, analyze CCTV footage and recognize vehicle 
number plates, etc. Big data can be used to integrate and store data from multiple sources. 
This will help in developing a scientific approach to policing. The Committee recommends 
that the MHA may encourage and incentivize States to leverage technologies like artificial 
intelligence, big data, etc. for policing. The Committee further recommends that BPR&D 
may be tasked to make a compendium of the latest technologies used by the various State 
police forces and share among them. This will help the States to fight crimes in a coordinated 
manner. 
(Para  3.17.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.2 This Ministry shares the same view. This Ministry will continue to leverage 
technologies like artificial intelligence, big data analysis, etc., for policing by the State / UT 
Governments under the scheme of ‘Assistance to States and UTs for Modernisation of 
Police’. 

 
7 
 
1.6.3 BPR&D regularly publishes a Compendium of Equipment purchased by various 
police organisations.  As recommended by the Committee, BPR&D has been asked to make a 
compendium of the latest technologies used by the various State police forces and share 
among them. 
Further Recommendation  
1.6.4 The Committee notes the reply. 
1.7 Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.7.1  The Committee notes that Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) is a Pan-
